25. Loss on a policy underwritten by a testator cannot be set off against amount due to executors.

§ 185. Set-off cannot be claimed of a loss on a policy underwritten by a testator, with a broker, against the amount due to the executors from the broker for premiums. There is no right, either at law or in equity, to deduct a loss on a policy underwritten by a testator with a broker from the amount due to the executors for premiums from the same broker, though the circumstances are such as in case of bankruptcy, would support a plea of mutual credit.

A custom that in case of the death of an underwriter, the premiums should be retained until all the risks had run off, might give such a right. But the English Court of Queen’s Bench, in a case where they had the power to draw inferences of fact from the evidence, drew the inference that such a custom did not exist at Lloyds.

(a) Houstoun v. Bordenave, 6 Taunt. 451.

An underwriter having subscribed a policy, and thereby confessed the receipt of the premium, is estopped from afterwards claiming the premium against the assured, and cannot, in an action brought against him by the assured for a loss, set off the premium, unless he can make it appear that the state of the relative accounts between assured broker and underwriter, is such as to take the case out of the ordinary rule, which is, that the receipt of the underwriter is conclusive evidence for the assured that he has paid the premium to the underwriter (De Gaminde v. Pigou, 4 Taunt. 246). But if by the fraud of the assured, the underwriter is induced to give credit for the premiums to the broker, and the broker to give credit to the assured, the underwriter is entitled to receive the premiums from the assured.

§ 186. An underwriter cannot set off as a mutual credit in an action against him for a loss accruing after policies of insurance, effected by Gordon as agent for the plaintiff, upon four ships. The plaintiff claimed a loss upon one of them of 99. 48. 4d. per cent., amounting, upon the defendant's subscription, to 297/. 18s., and a return of 10 per cent. upon the defendant’s subscriptions on the other ships for convoy and arrival, amounting to 90/. more, making, together, the sum of 3871. 18s. The defendant gave notice of set-off for the premiums upon these very policies, and for the premium of another policy effected by the plaintiff through the same agent with the defendant on another ship, together amounting to 582/. 15s. Upon the trial of the cause, it appeared that the plaintiff, who resided at Pillan, procured Gordon, who was a young man just embarking in business, to effect the several policies in question, upon an assurance that he would address the ships to him and permit him to receive the freight and reimburse himself thereout for the amount of the premiums. Upon a communication of this proposal to the underwriters, they gave Gordon credit for the premiums. The plaintiff also remitted to Gordon, whom he had drawn into other transactions with him, bills on Thornton and Bayley, which the latter refused to accept, alleging that they waited for some explanation from the plaintiff, but that all would be right; and in the meantime offered to accommodate the plaintiff by accepting his own bills for the like amount upon the security of these policies which Gordon accordingly deposited in their hands. The plaintiff, instead of consigning his ships to Gordon, as he had promised, consigned them to Thornton and Bayley, and assigned the freight to them, so that Gordon was left destitute, as well of the means of receiving the loss and returns of premiums as of the expected funds to arise from the freight for the payment of the premiums to the underwriters. The defendant, therefore, now claimed to set off the premiums which he had never received against the loss and returns to which he was liable. The jury, thinking that when the underwriter signs a policy and thereby acknowledges the receipt of the premium, the account is finally closed between the assured and the underwriter, found a verdict for the plaintiff. Upon a motion for a new trial, which was granted, the court said: “The jury were strongly impressed in this case with the general doctrine that the transaction is closed when the underwriter writes his receipt, and that he cannot afterwards say the premium has not been paid. But the plaintiff knew, as appeared by his own letters, that Gordon was perfectly unable to pay these premiums. The plaintiff had prevailed upon him to effectuate these policies, in effecting which, he knew that Gordon, according to the common course of business, got receipts for this immense sum, and he knew that the defendant must give these receipts. The plaintiff knew that Gordon had no fund out of which that money could have been paid. He knew that, according to the course of business, though receipts were to be given by the underwriters who subscribed the policies, yet, in fact, no money had ever passed between the underwriter and broker. He knew he had promised to put into his

An executor or administrator cannot set off a demand purchased by him.

§ 187. As the duty of an executor or administrator is to settle the estate, pay the debts, and distribute the surplus, and not to speculate in demands against creditors, he cannot set off a debt purchased by him since the death of the testator or intestate, against a demand.

* In Glennie et als. v. But I can find no case which furnishes a principle for it.”

“The assured cannot, without the consent of the underwriter, impose upon him any responsibility to a third person, whereby the rights of the underwriter will be impaired, or his liability enhanced; or will be modified in any respect any further than to put him under obligation, after notice, to be accountable to the assignee for the amount for which he is liable under the policy. Whatever set-off he was entitled to at the time of notice of the assignment, and whatever other defense he could make against the original assured he may still make, notwithstanding the assignment” (Phillips on Ins., 5th ed. vol. 1, sect. 82).

Where there is an assignment of a policy with the consent of the insurers, “reserving all rights of set-off,” the reservation applies to contracts or liabilities existing at the date of the assignment (Phillips on Ins., vol. 1, sect. 196).

Mr. Phillips (Ins. 5th ed. vol. 1, sect. 903) says: “It is a frequent stipulation in policies, and often in the consent to assignments of them, that the underwriters shall have the right to set off demands, for premiums or otherwise, against losses.”

It was held in New York, in Diehl v. Genl. Mu. Ins. Co., 1 Sandf. 257, that where the demand for loss was at the time of the assignment of the policy unliquidated, it could not be the subject of set-off between the assignees and the underwriters. But it seems that in Pennsylvania a demand which was unliquidated at the time of the assignment may be set off. The latter rule prevails in England, where it is held that an underwriter may set off premiums on policies made before the bankruptcy of the assured against losses occurring after the bankruptcy on policies of date prior to it (Phillips on Ins., sect. 903; Rousset v. “At law, a testamentary act cannot operate as a release of a debt owing to the testator; but in a court of equity it may sometimes have the effect of extinguishing the debt. A mere bequest, however, of a legacy by a creditor to his debtor is not necessarily, or even prima facie a release or extinguishment. The court requires evidence clearly expressive of such an intention before it will give effect to the act. If this intention is not expressed or rendered apparent on the face of the will, then evidence aliunde will be admitted to prove an intention to release or discharge it” (2 Roper on Legacies, 87, 62, 64; Vice-Chancellor in Stagg v. § 190 A LEGACY TO A DEBTOR. 235

In such cases, seeks to obtain a portion of the fund which the testator, or the letters of administration, have placed in the hands of the executor or administrator which is equal to, or greater than the debt, shall be considered as a satisfaction of it. But this is merely a rule of construction, and the courts in a variety of instances have denied the application of it where they have been able to collect from the will circumstances to repel the presumption. As where it contains an express direction for the payment of debts; or if the legacy be less than the debt it has been held not to go in discharge nor even in diminution of it. Nor shall the legacy be a satisfaction if it be conditional, or given on a contingency, for it shall not be supposed that the testator intended an uncertain recompense in satisfaction of a certain demand. Nor is a legacy considered as a satisfaction where it is not equally beneficial with the debt in one respect, though it may be more so in another; as where the legacy is to a greater amount, but the payment of it is postponed for however short a period; nor shall a legacy be held to be in satisfaction of a covenant unless it be equally beneficial in amount, certainty, and time of enjoyment, with the thing contracted for. Nor if the debt were on an open or running account, so that the testator could not tell whether the balance was in favor of the legatee or not. Nor if the debt were contracted after the making of the will in which the legacy is given, shall he be supposed to have had it in contemplation to satisfy a debt that was not then in existence. But in all cases, the legacy shall be construed as a satisfaction in case there be a deficiency of assets (Toller's Exrs, 836, 438, and cases cited; and see Eaton v. Benton, 2 Hill, 576).

“When a legacy has been decreed to go in satisfaction of a debt, it must be grounded upon some evidence or at least a strong presumption that the testator so intended it. A court of equity will carry into effect the intention of the testator, and therefore the intention is what controls. In Cranmer’s case, 2 Salk. 508, the testatrix owed Cranmer £50, and made a will giving him a legacy of £500, she then borrowed £150 more, and died. The master of the rolls held the legacy a payment of both debts. But the Lord Chancellor reversed the decree, saying that a man shall not be prevented by a court of equity from doing with his own as he pleases; and when he says he gives a legacy, they cannot say he pays a debt.” See opinion of the court in Williams v. Crary, 4 Wend. 443. The rule with some of its exceptions will be found in Nicholls v. Judson, 2 Atk. 300; 2 Ves. Sen. 635; Chancey’s Case, 1 P. Wms. 410, N. 1; 2 P. Wms. 553; 3 Tb. 355; Clarke v. Bogardus, 12 Wend. 67.

“Parol declarations by the testator are admissible in evidence to repel the presumption of the satisfaction of the debt, by the bequest of a legacy of greater amount, even where such declarations were not contemporaneous with, but subsequent to the making of the will; and although the expressions in the will may afford an inference in favor of the presumption” (Toller's Exrs. 338).

According to Mr. Williams (Tr. on Exrs, 1167) the rule established in courts of equity, that where a debtor bequeathes to his creditor a legacy equal to, or exceeding the amount of his debt, it shall be presumed in the absence of any intimation of a contrary intention, that the legacy was meant by the testator as a satisfaction of the debt, though it has long prevailed, has met with the censure of several eminent judges; and the courts have inclined to lay hold of minute circumstances whereupon to ground an exception to it.

30. Set off of debt against legacy to wife of debtor.

§ 191. Where a debt to the estate of a testator may be set off by the executors against a legacy of such indebtedness; it being his proportion of all the latter's personal estate as one of the next of kin. But it was held that the proper credit to be made for the interest of I. H. in his father’s estate as next of kin was one-ninth of two-thirds, instead of one-ninth of the personal estate; and that the executors of I. H. had no control over the right or interest of I. H. as legatee or next of kin in his mother's estate, and could not withhold her share of the personal estate of I. H. from her administrator, on the ground that a part of it would belong to I. H., and he was indebted in a greater sum to his father’s executors. The assistant Vice Chancellor (Sandford) said: "The complainants have never had in their hands belonging to Isaac Hone any more than one-ninth of two-thirds of the personal property. While the widow lived the other third belonged to her. On her death, it passed to her executor or administrator. He had a perfect right to demand it from the complainants. They could not resist the administrator’s demand by showing that Isaac was indebted to them in a larger sum, and that he would be entitled to receive a like sum from the administrator as legatee or next of kin of his mother. In the strongest point of view in which the defendants can present it, the case is this. "The complainants owe to Mrs. Hone’s administrator one-third of their testator’s personal property, which third I will assume to be $80,000.00. The administrator is bound to pay one-ninth of that sum to Isaac, and I will call that a debt from him to Isaac of $9,000.00. Isaac owes to the complainants, as such executors, $18,000.00 for example. And upon this, it is claimed that the complainants may retain from the administrator towards Isaac's debt, the $9,000 which the administrator is to pay the latter; or, in other words, they may pay $9,000 of their debt to the administrator in Isaac’s debt to them; thus making an offset of Isaac's debt to their own creditor because the latter is Isaac’s debtor. It seems manifest to me that no such right of set-off exists either at law or in equity. If on his mother’s death, Isaac has sold his interest in her estate; or, as was stated to be the fact in this case, had assigned it for the benefit of creditors, such an offset as is attempted here would not avail the administrator in a suit by his vendee or assignee."

In Howland v. Heckscher, supra, "it was urged that Isaac’s debt to his father’s estate was a component part of his mother’s third of the personalty, and as such came to her administrator. But this is not true in point of law. Mrs. Hone was entitled to a third, not in this or that specific stock, security, or debt, in which the personalty happened to be at the testator’s death, but to money. She might accept stock or securities, but she could neither compel their delivery nor be compelled to take them. Isaac was never a debtor to her or to her administrator in respect of this debt, either legally or equitably. So far as it was collected, she was entitled to her third of the proceeds; and so, from time to time, as collections should be made. But such third she would receive as and towards her distributive share of the estate of John Hone, and in no sense as a creditor of Isaac.

"The simple and direct mode of ascertaining how much the complainants ought to credit to Isaac in respect of his father’s personal estate was this: From the gross amount of the personalty, including Isaac’s debt de-

Under that law there was reason and equity in adopting such a course. It prevented circuity of action and secured to the estate a debt which would otherwise have been entirely lost where the husband was insolvent. So much of the debt of a legatee to the testator, including the interest due at the time of the death of the latter as can be collected by the administrator, must be considered and treated as a part of the capital of the testator’s estate, and must be apportioned and distributed accordingly. If the whole amount of the debt and interest could be received by such retainer of income, so much as had accrued for interest since the death of the testator would be properly distributable among those who had present interests in the personal estate; and the sum due at the death of the testator would all be considered and treated as a part of the capital of his estate.

It applies to cases where the maker, who is also payee, negotiates the note without indorsement. (a) Sears v. Patrick, 23 Wend. 528.

* “In common cases of a dissolution, it is competent for the partners to agree between themselves, either originally by their articles of partnership, or by their arrangements at its dissolution, that one partner may or shall take the whole partnership property at a valuation; and the assignment thereof, when made bona fide in either way, will be valid and obligatory upon the creditors. While the partnership is solvent and going on, the creditors have no equity, strictly speaking, against the effects of the partnership. Neither have they any lien on the partnership effects for their debts. All they can or may do, is to proceed by an action at law for their debts against the partners, and having obtained judgment therein, they may cause the execution issuing upon that judgment to be levied upon the partnership effects, or upon the separate effects of each partner, or upon others. There being, then, no lien, and no equity in favor of the creditors against the partnership effects, until such execution is issued and levied thereon, it follows that those effects are susceptible of being legally transferred bona fide for a valuable consideration to any persons whatsoever, and as well to other partners as to mere strangers. And this is equally true, although the whole, or a part of the consideration of the transfer is, that the partners taking the property shall pay the whole or a particular part of the debts of the partnership. But in cases of bankruptcy, it is otherwise” (Story on Part., § 306, 358, 359).

§205 ACTION BY ONE OF SEVERAL PARTNERS. 253

A firm, in order to secure creditors, agreed to transfer to them thirteen coal barges with the furniture, a lot of harness, &c., and executed a bill of sale therefor. At the same time, one of the firm covenanted to sell and convey to the creditors certain real estate belonging to him, in consideration of which, the creditors agreed to pay the liens thereon which were for his individual debts. The creditors took possession of the land, but soon afterwards abandoned the same, and it was sold by the sheriff on the liens. In an action by the individual partner against the creditors, on their agreement to take his land and pay the liens, the defendants insisted that it and the bill of sale were parts of the same transaction, and that they had a right to set off against the amount claimed against them damages for breach of the partnership in not turning over to them the personal property sold. Lowrie, C. J., in delivering the opinion of the court, said: “Though there is partial unity in the transaction, yet there is also a formal and substantial duplicity; one part relating to partnership debts, and the other to the private debts of one of the partners."

It was contended in behalf of the defendant that the representations of the plaintiff at the time of the sale were made by the plaintiff individually, and not by the firm of H. and S., and it did not appear that S. knew of them or of the defective character of the machinery, while the plaintiff did; that the case ought, therefore, to stand as if the plaintiff owned the machinery alone, and he having injured the defendant by his misrepresentations, should suffer for it. On the other hand, the plaintiff took the ground that recoupment or set-off could not be allowed because of the misrepresentations of the plaintiff at the time of the sale of the machinery; that the representations were by H. and S. as partners; and any claim the defendant might have on their account was a joint one against them as partners and could not be set off in a suit by one of them, the parties being different; that damage for false representations was all that the defendant could claim; and from the very nature of the transaction, those damages must be unliquidated, and therefore could not be the subject of set-off or recoupment. The court remarked that if the plaintiff knew the character of the machinery and did not inform his employer of it, that might, under some circumstances, amount to negligence in the performance of the work; but that any claim growing out of unskillful or negligent workmanship had been considered and allowed.

* In Maine, in an action by an administrator, it was contended in behalf of the defendant that he might set off a demand against the intestate and three other persons still living. Defendant's counsel did not rely upon such a construction of the statute as would have allowed his demand to be set off in an action in favor of the deceased in his lifetime; but insisted that his death had caused a severance of the claim which was before joint; that an action could be maintained thereon against the plaintiff as administrator, and that, therefore, the same claim might be legally set off. It was held, however, that it could not be done (Adams v. Ware, 33 Maine, 228). The court said: “It was manifestly the intention of the legislature to limit the operation of the statute to the demands between the parties during the lifetime of both; and that no change should be effected by the death of either in this respect, excepting by the substitution of the executor or administrator for the deceased. It was clearly the design of the statute in relation to set-off, that there should not be a separation of demands, which were joint against the original debtors, by the death of one of them, although a severance might be the consequence of the death; and the same rule was intended to apply under the statute, by or against an executor or administrator and the one whom he represents.”

(a) Holbrook v. Lackey, 18 Metc. 182; Trannelle v. Harrell, 4 Pike, 602; Miller v. Receiver of Franklin Bank, 1 Paige, R. 444.

(b) 13 Mass. R. 496.

* In Holbrook v. Lackey, supra, Chief Justice Shaw, in delivering the opinion of the court, said: “It was strongly pressed by the plaintiffs counsel, that to allow this set-off, would be to authorize the appropriation of partnership funds to pay the private debt of one of the partners, to the injury of partnership creditors. But this argument is specious rather than sound. We are not to presume necessarily that there are outstanding partnership debts, or that the funds are not ample to meet them.

“But how does it affect the partnership creditors? If the surviving partner could recover the whole without the deduction of the demand which the defendant seeks to set off, he would be liable indeed to pay the partnership debts, if there are any. But he would be equally liable without; and in either case, these creditors must look alone to his personal liability, and would have no means of compelling him to appropriate the specific money so recovered, to the payment of their debts.”

“The general rule of the common law certainly is that a debt due to partners is due to them jointly; and upon the death of one the sole right survives to the other. It is true that the survivor collects partnership debts under a liability to account; but at law he is the sole creditor, and has the sole power to collect the debt, and to maintain a suit to recover it. And all the legal consequences resulting from this principle are held to flow from it. The surviving partner in suing may join a separate debt of his own (8 T. R. 488). So a surviving partner in a suit against him for a separate debt of his own may set off a debt due to him and his deceased partner jointly (5 T. R. 493). So a debt from the plaintiff, as surviving partner, may be set off against a debt due from the defendant to the plaintiff severally (6 T. R. 582). In Massachusetts, it has been held that a surviving partner of two firms may join demands of both in one suit. It is so far held his duty to do so, that he can have but one bill of costs if he brings two actions. It is not the less a debt due to him in his own right, because, when collected, he may be personally liable to account for it on settlement of the partnership account, as for other payments made to him as partner. The section of the statute which provides that the demand to be set off must be due to the defendant in his own right, manifestly refers to cases of executors, administrators, trustees, and all parties suing or being sued in a representative capacity.”

§ 207. So, likewise, as to the converse of the foregoing proposition. That is, in an action by a surviving partner for his individual claim, the defendant may set off a demand against the firm.

French v. Andrade was an action of assumpsit brought by a surviving partner for his individual claim. To which the defendant pleaded that the plaintiff, and one J. M., who died before the commencement of the action, were indebted to the defendant in divers sums.

* “At law, where one of two joint obligees, covenantees, or partners, dies, the action on the contract must be brought in the name of the survivor, and the executor or administrator of the deceased cannot be joined, nor can he sue separately. And although the right of a dead partner devolves on his executor, yet the remedy survives to his companion, who alone must enforce the right by action, subject to account to the representatives of the deceased. It follows, that where a contract is made jointly with several persons, and they all die, the executor or administrator of the survivor alone can sue, and the personal representatives of those who died before him cannot be joined. And in equity, the survivor and representatives of the deceased cannot join as plaintiffs, upon the principle that parties cannot be co-plaintiffs who have or may have hostile interests” (Dunlap’s Paleys Agency, p. 53, note).

+ As at law the remedy to recover on choses in action belonging to the partnership survives, it follows that the surviving partner may set off a debt due to him as such, against a demand on him in his own right.

So, the defendant may set off a debt due by the plaintiff as surviving partner against a demand due to him in his own right.

So far, the rights of the representatives of the deceased partner, and of the partnership creditors, are not affected. Where the surviving partner is a defendant, he may set off a partnership claim, because, as respects the plaintiff, he may treat it as his own. So, where a person who is a surviving partner, sues for his separate debt, the defendant may set off a partnership debt against it.

But there is no case to show that where the suit is for a debt due to the partnership, the defendant can set off a debt separately due by the plaintiff. For though a surviving partner may choose to treat a partnership debt as due to him in his own right, it does not follow that a defendant, sued for a debt separately due, has a corresponding right. And even if he had such a right at law, a court of equity, if the surviving partner were insolvent, would doubtless interfere to prevent it from being exercised; and this on the same ground that it interferes to prevent an insolvent surviving partner from disposing of the stock, or getting in the outstanding debts (Waln. v. Hewes, 5 Serg. & R. 467).

There is a distinction at common law between partnership property, and effects in possession, and choses in action, debts, and other rights of action belonging to the partnership. “The latter, at law, belong to the surviving partners, and they possess the sole and exclusive right to reduce them into possession; although, when so recovered, the survivors are regarded as trustees thereof for the benefit of the partnership, and the representatives of the deceased partner possess in equity the same right of sharing and participating in them which the deceased partner would have possessed if he had been living” (Story on Part. § 346).

§ 212 ONE OF SEVERAL LIABLE FOR PAYMENT.

1 Set-off of judgment where each one of several is liable for the payment of it.

§ 212. Where each one of several defendants against whom a judgment is rendered is liable for the payment of the entire demand, such judgment may be set off against a judgment obtained by one of the defendants against the holder of the first-mentioned judgment.

In a case in which this principle was discussed, Parker, Ch. J., in delivering the opinion of the court, said: “The demand of the defendant (a) being a joint debt of the plaintiff and another, is not a mutual claim which he could file in set-off as a matter of right under the statute. But if he now had a judgment on that claim against the plaintiff and the other signer of the note, the plaintiff being liable for the payment of the entire demand, the court might set off the defendant’s judgment against that of the plaintiff, if the equity of the case required it. And we are of opinion that it will be a proper exercise of discretion to continue the plaintiff’s action for judgment until the defendant can have an opportunity to obtain a judgment on his note for the purpose of making this set-off. If, as it seems, the plaintiff owes the debt, and be irresponsible, there will certainly be no justice in his collecting his demand as any individual debt as any one he can owe. It is true there is an equitable rule which would compel the partnership funds to be exhausted for partnership debts. But before an individual creditor can claim any benefit from it, he must show that there are such assets which can be pursued. Here there is no proof to warrant the belief of the existence of such assets, even if a court of law was competent to arrest their due application.”

8. Individual debt against partnership demand.

§ 2138. We have seen (d) that in an action by one of a firm for his individual claim, a demand against the firm cannot be set off. So, on the other hand, in an action by a firm for a partnership claim, a demand against one of the partners individually, is not, excepting under circumstances to which we shall presently advert, a proper offset. (c) *

(c) Watson v. Hensel, 7 Watts, 844; S. P. Archer v. Dunne, 2 Watts & Serg. 827; Kenedy v. Cunningham, Cheves, 50. See post, §§ 214-218.

* In Massachusetts, the Statute (Genl. Sts. ed. of 1860, p. 670) provides that, except in the case of a dormant partner, “If there are several plaintiffs, the demand set off shall be due from all of them jointly; and if there are several defendants, the demand set off shall be due to all of them jointly.”

The question as to whether a claim in a given case is joint or several may, under certain circumstances, be of difficult solution. It does not necessarily follow because two persons who are not partners have joined together to make a purchase for a joint shipment, that they will be jointly liable to the vendor for the purchase money; for if the purchase has been made under circumstances that demonstrate that the vendor gave an exclusive credit to each of them for a moiety, then each will be solely and separately liable only for his own share. And the same rule may be justly applicable to cases of partnership, where such a division of the credit is authorized and acted upon by the vendor, with a clear understanding that it is to be an exclusive credit pro tanto. The case of a debt contracted prior to the existence of a partnership has also sometimes been treated as a case where exclusive credit is given to the contracting party, and not to the firm, although they ultimately receive the benefit thereof. But it may be resolved into the more general principle that a contract can be obligatory only upon those who are parties to it, or derive benefit from it at the time of its inception. Neither at law nor in equity can such a set-off be maintained upon that mere footing. The partnership was not liable for the separate debt of one of the partners; nor bound to contribute towards its payment. There is no equity to compel a partnership to pay the separate debts of a partner founded upon the mere fact of that relation. On the contrary, the doctrine is just as clear in equity as at law, that joint debts cannot be set off against separate debts or separate debts against joint debts; for they accrue in different rights. But then it is said that here C. is and was insolvent at the time of the payment of the joint judgment by W., and that of itself creates an equity for a set-off. Whether in a case of mutual debts in the same right—as for example, mutual joint debts, or mutual separate debts, the insolvency of either party will entitle the other to set off his debt against the debt of the insolvent party without any other intervening equity, is a point not necessary to be decided. Natural equity would seem to urge such a set-off in such a case; for, otherwise, the insolvent party might recover his whole debt, and the other party might recover a dividend only, or, indeed, nothing. Yet there is no reason to doubt, even in such a case, whether the courts of equity in England ever admitted a set-off founded upon the mere fact of insolvency. In ex parte Prescott (1 Atk. 281), Lord Hardwicke affirmed the contrary; and said that in cases of bankruptcy before the statute of the 5th Geo. 2, ch. 80, if there were eventual debts, the creditor could not set off the debt due to him against the debt due from him to the bankrupt even in equity.

But in the case of a joint debt the same reasoning could not apply in favor of the set-off of the separate debt of one of the partners; at least not until all the joint debts were paid and all the equities of the other partner were satisfied. For it is a general rule that no partner has any separate interest except in the surplus of the partnership property after the payment of all the joint debts and other equities. If there should be such a surplus, the same rule might apply.

Where he said, “If A and B. are joint traders, and J. S. owes A. and B. on their joint account £100, and A. owes the said J. S. £100 on his separate account, J. S. cannot deduct so much as A.’s proportion of the £100 comes to out of the joint debt; for the co-partnership debts of A. and B. are to be first paid before any of the separate debts. But if there be a surplus beyond what will pay the partnership debts, then out of A.’s share of the surplus J. S. may deduct the separate debt of A. The strong inclination of my mind is that, according to the present course of decisions, courts of equity in England will not entertain a set-off of a separate debt of one partner against a joint debt due to the partnership, upon the mere ground of the insolvency of that partner; for it must necessarily involve a settlement of all the partnership debts and an ascertainment of all the partnership equities before any relief can be given. The case of Simson v. Hart, 14 John. R. 63, is apparently the other way, and affirms that insolvency does or may constitute a sufficient equity to entitle a party who is a creditor upon a joint judgment to set off that judgment against a separate judgment debt due by him to one of the joint judgment debtors, both of the latter being insolvent. The ground of the decision seems to have been that the party having the joint judgment and who applied for the relief had the sole interest in the judgment.

“In the present case, the right of set-off could not exist against C. and D. so long as the latter possessed any interest in the judgment. When that judgment was assigned to the U.S. the latter were clothed with all the rights and interests of the partnership, provided the assignment made by C. in his own name and in D.’s name was an operative conveyance as to both; that is, provided C. had authority from D. to make the assignment.”

“The right of set-off on the part of W. is gone, or rather, never had any real existence. That right was not an equity attached to the original judgment of C. and D. It was a right which at most could be asserted against C. only, when he should become the exclusive owner in law or equity of that judgment, and while he was so owner. The assignment of that judgment to the U.S. extinguished all the legal and equitable interest of C., as well as of D., in it; and the U.S. became bona fide purchasers of it for a valuable consideration. The equity of the U.S. then is both prior in point of time and better in point of right than that of W. in regard to the judgment. Where there are mutual debts, which may be set off, in law or equity, the right of set-off is extinguished by a bona fide assignment of one of the debts. I cannot find that there ever was a moment in which C. was the exclusive owner of the joint judgment; and unless he was, there never could, according to the principles already stated, exist a right in W. to set off his separate debt against the joint judgment at law or in equity.”

In England it has been held, that if, after a partnership is dissolved, and the partnership debts are paid, a surplus remains, a person who is indebted to the partnership, and is also a separate creditor of either of the partners against whom a commission of bankruptcy has issued, may set off the joint debt against the surplus to which the bankrupt is entitled.

Where a suit is brought by a husband and wife to recover a legacy bequeathed to the wife, and a judgment is rendered therein jointly in their behalf, it is not such a reducing of the legacy into possession by the husband, as that another judgment recovered by the defendant against the husband alone can be set off against the first mentioned judgment (Crittenden and wife v. Alexander, 15 Gray, 482). Merrick, J.: ‘It is a general and well settled principle of law, that a set-off is allowable only in those cases in which the parties to the record, or the real parties in interest are the same. But that was not the condition or relation of the parties to each other in the present suits. The amount recovered by the plaintiffs was upon a claim on a legacy bequeathed to the wife; and although her husband had such interest in and right to it, that he might by reducing it to possession, make it his own, yet until he did that, her right to it was not extinguished. In fact, he never did reduce it to possession; for a suit in the name of himself and wife, and a judgment thereon jointly in their behalf, will not have such an effect. If the husband should in such case die before collecting the money or enforcing the judgment, the wife would, as survivor, take the whole benefit of it, and hold it to her own sole use, for her interest and right remain until the husband has, by some competent and sufficient act, reduced the demand to his own possession.”

Although a legacy to the wife may, under the Statutes of Massachusetts, be taken by an attachment in a suit against the husband and transferred by virtue of it in the payment of his debts; yet “even in that case, it is held to be a chose in action which survives to the wife, if the husband die pending the suit or before levy of the execution. Upon his decease, the lien created by the attachment is necessarily dissolved; and the wife will then, as survivor, hold and recover the legacy to her own use. If there be no collection of the money due, and no legal assignment or transfer of the legacy, nothing short of a judgment in a suit by the husband in his own name for its recovery, will amount to such a reduction to possession, as will bar the wife’s right of survivorship.”

The court in Sillivant v. Reardon, supra, said: “The true question is not as to the mutuality of indebtedness of the parties to the action as they remain upon the record, but of the mutuality of indebtedness as it existed between the parties at the time of the commencement of the suit. If, when Reardon commenced the suit against the defendants, he really owed them six hundred dollars as pleaded, can he avoid the set-off by abandoning his action as to one? To admit such a rule would be to admit the worst consequences of suffering a discontinuance. We now decide that where a plaintiff sues one or more of several joint obligors or joint promisers, and his declaration shows that the parties so sued, together with the co-obligors or promisers not sued, have a meritorious offset against the plaintiff, that the parties so sued may plead the offset which might properly be pleaded by all the obligors or promisers were they parties to the record. Should we analogize this defense to other pleas to the action, our view of the subject would gain great strength. Just as a payment by a party not sued would be a good discharge to those sued, so would accord and satisfaction, release and some others.”

The question then arises whether a judgment for the balance which appears to be due from the plaintiff to Joseph S. and John Mott, can be rendered in this case, as John Mott is not before the Court, and is not now a party to the suit. We are inclined to the opinion that a judgment may be rendered for this balance in the name of Joseph S., the only defendant who appears; and that in order to carry the provisions of the statute into effect, in a case situated like this, judgment must be so rendered. The demand due from the plaintiff was due to them jointly. Either could have controlled it, or commenced an action thereon in the name of both. Either could have received payment, released or receipted the whole demand, accounting to the other for his share.”

The statute of Minnesota of 1851 (Comp. St. p. 571, sect. 106) provides that: “Any real or personal estate which may have been acquired by any female before her marriage, either by her own personal industry or by inheritance, gift, or devise, to which she may at any time after her marriage be entitled by inheritance, gift, grant, or devise, and the rents, profits, and income of any such real estate, shall be and continue the real and personal estate of such female after marriage to the same extent as before marriage; and none of such property shall be liable for her husband’s debts, engagements, or liabilities; provided, that nothing in this section contained shall be construed to authorize any married woman to give, grant, or sell any such real or personal property, during coveture, without the consent of her husband, except by order of the District Court of the county.”

In Carpenter v. Leonard, supra, the court remarked that the object of the foregoing statute was “to relieve married women of the disabilities of coveture in regard to the use, enjoyment, and disposal of their property, acquired as provided in the statute, and whether the estate be legal or equitable. And it has done this to the fullest extent, except in so far as the statute itself has imposed restrictions; and the only restriction imposed upon her action in this regard is, that she is not permitted to give, grant, or sell any such real or personal property during coveture, without the consent of her husband, except by order of the District Court of the county. Aside from this, the property is hers to the same extent as before marriage. As a feme sole may use and improve her property, so by this statute, may the married woman; and if, as an incident of such use and improvement, the property itself becomes liable to pay her debts in the same manner as it would be liable if she were sole, it furnishes no reason for the construction that she is to be limited in the use and enjoyment in such manner that such liability shall not ensue. On the contrary, it may reasonably be inferred from the terms of the statute itself, that it was the intent to make the property liable for her debts, since it expressly makes it so for all debts of the wife contracted before marriage, and provides that she may be divested of title by order of the District Court without the consent of her husband.”

(a) Columbia Ins. Co. v. Black, 18 Johns. 149.

* Columbia Ins. Co. v. Black, supra, was an action on a note payable to the defendant or his order, and indorsed by him to the plaintiffs for premiums of insurance underwritten by the plaintiffs in the name of the defendant for the owners, on the freight of the schooner Fanny. The defendant was allowed to set off a total loss incurred on a valued policy of insurance on the freight of the schooner Dick, underwritten by the plaintiffs for the defendant for account of the owners, notice of abandonment having been duly given with the usual proofs of interest and loss, but no adjustment made. Spencer, Ch. J., in delivering the opinion of the court, said; “The facts in the present case are simple and few, and are not calculated to produce a perplexed inquiry. The liquidation of damages depends on the sailing of the vessel with a cargo, and her loss by a peril insured against. A set-off here promotes justice and prevents litigation; and no case can come before the court in which the injustice of denying the set-off would be more glaring. It cannot be seriously doubted that the defendant alone could sustain a suit for the loss. It was an insurance for him on account of the owners of the schooner. The contract is between these parties, and although all the owners might unite in a suit, the defendant is competent to sue alone, and then the principle applies that if legal or equitable claims or liabilities become vested in one person, they may be set off against separate demands, and so vice versa.”

In Parker v. Beasley, 2 Maul. & Sel. 428, the defendants were sued for premiums of insurance, and at the trial offered to set off the losses on two policies underwritten by the bankrupt, whose assignees the plaintiffs were. The defendants effected the policies in their own names. But other persons were proprietors in different proportions of the cargo. Lord Ellenborough held (the other Judges concurring) that the policies being effected in the name of the brokers on account of other persons, the brokers could maintain an action in their own names if they had any lien on the policies; and by subscribing to policies in their own names, the underwriters had consented that they might stand in the character and situation of principals.

In the last mentioned case, it was not objected that the loss on the policy could not be set off. But it was agreed on all hands that it could be done if the defendants had a right to avail themselves of the policy.

With regard to the setting off of a joint demand, it has several times been decided in Pennsylvania, that such a claim may be set off by one of the owners in an action against him for his own proper debt, provided he have the express assent of his co-partners, and there are no third interests to be prejudiced. Accordingly, where the defendant bought a judgment against A., who then held as payee a promissory note, the credit of the assignor, I would not only allow a set-off against the party to the record and the party in interest, but against every party through whose hands it has thus passed.

The indorsee of a note overdue takes it with notice on its face that it is discredited, and, therefore, subject to all payments and offsets in the nature of payments. He takes the note subject to all the equities between the prior parties (Bond v. Fitzpatrick, 4 Gray, 89, per Dewey, J., citing Baxter v. Little, 6 Metc. 10; Sargent v. Southgate, 5 Pick. 312. And see Little v. Cooper, 8 Stockt. 224; Farrir v. Catlett, 32 Mis. 469; Lord v. Favorite, 29 Ill. 149; Kurz v. Holbrook, 18 Iowa, 562; White v. Heylman, 34 Penn. St. R. 142).

The English rule is that the indorser of a bill or note is liable to such equities only as attach on the bill or note itself, and not to claims arising out of collateral matters. In Oulds v. Harrison, 28 Eng. L. & Eq. R. 524, Parke, B., in delivering the opinion of the court, said: “It must be considered as entirely settled, by the case of Burrough v. Moss, 10 B. & C. 558, that the indorsee of an overdue bill takes it subject to all equities that attach to the bill itself in the hands of the holder when it was due; as, for instance, payment or satisfaction of the bill itself to such holder; or where the title of such holder was to secure a lien upon the bill for the amount of an unsettled account. But the indorsee does not take it subject to the claim arising out of collateral matters. There are cases where the bill has been paid, or where the lien has been created on the bill in the hands of the holder at the time it is due. In that case, the subsequent taker of the bill must take it subject to repayment or right of action, or that lien, whatever it may be; but the indorsee does not take it subject to the claim arising out of collateral matters. The doctrine that was laid down in Burrough v. Moss has been followed in the case of Stein v. Yglesias, 1 Cr. M. & R. 565. The notice of the existence of the set-off to the holder of the bill at the time it was due makes no difference, as was settled in the case of Whitehead v. Walker, 10 Mees & W. 696, unless, indeed, express notice was given by the party liable, and evidence of an acquiescence, such as would amount to proof of an agreement to let in the set-off assented to by both parties; and then it would be in satisfaction of the bill, and depend entirely upon the statute itself.”

The English rule mentioned above does not prevail very generally in the United States. In general in this country, an independent demand may be set off where in other respects the party is entitled to go into that defense (Sargent v. Southgate, 5 Pick. 312; Ranger v. Cary, 1 Metc, 375; Edw. on Bills and Notes, 260. But see contra, Shipman v. Robbins, 10 ae R. 208; Mattoon v. McDaniel, 834 Mis. 138; Arnot v. Woodburn, 35 is, 99).

The right of set-off against the payee of an overdue note which has been transferred depends upon the statute; a set-off in such case not being allowed at common law. In New York, where the plaintiff bought a negotiable promissory note of the payee after the note was due, and at the time of the purchase the payee was indebted to the maker, in an action by the holder against the maker it was held that the demand of the latter could not be set off against the holder; and that it was not, in any view, a defense to the action (Johnson agst. Bridge, 6 Cowen, 698). The defendant had paid the note in fact, or shown it was not valid in its origin,

§ 257 NOTE TRANSFERRED AFTER IT IS DUE. 303

note of the defendant, and A. afterwards, and after the note was due, transferred the note to the plaintiff, it was or otherwise discharged, before transfer, and after due, no difficulty would have lain in his way. But that was not the case. The ground of defense was a set-off which would have been unobjectionable in an action in the name of the payee; but it was not valid against the plaintiff, who sued in the character of indorser or bearer (Ib.)

In New York, the statute of set-off, as it was worded previous to the revision of the statutes, spoke of mutual debts only between the mutual parties to the suit. In O’Callaghan v. Sawyer, 5 John. R. 118, the plaintiff was assignee by indorsement of a promissory note; and the note being indorsed after it was due, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Common Pleas, because it excluded from the defense matter of set-off against the payee. Nearly twenty years afterwards that case was overruled in Johnson v. Bridge, supra, affd. 5 Wend. 342; but the latter decision was affirmed in the Court of Errors by only a tie vote (see Wheeler v. Raymond, 5 Cowen, 231).

The New York revised statutes (5th Ed., vol. 3, p. 685) provide that “if the action be upon a negotiable promissory note or bill of exchange which has been assigned to the plaintiff after it became due, a set-off to the amount of the plaintiff's debt may be made of a demand existing against any person or persons who shall have assigned or transferred such note or bill after it became due, if the demand be such as might have been set off against the assignor while the note or bill belonged to him.”

Under this statute, “if a negotiable promissory note be given by A. to B., which, after it has become due, is assigned or transferred by B. to C., and by C. to D., in an action on such note in the name of D. against A., he may set off to the amount due on the note only, either, first, a demand against B., the payee of the note, which was in existence at the time of the assignment or transfer of the note by B. to C., and which, if it were not originally due to A., had been at that time assigned to him; or, secondly, he may set off a demand against C. which was in existence at the time of the assignment or transfer by C. to D., and which, if it were not originally due to A., had been at that time assigned to him; or, thirdly, he may set off the whole of a demand against D., the plaintiff, which was in existence at the time of the commencement of the action, and then belonged to A. either as the original creditor or as the assignee thereof. But if the note had been transferred by B. to C. before it became due, then, in a suit in the name of D. against A., no set-off could be made of a demand against B., but a set-off could only be made of a demand against C. or D., as above stated. So, if the note had been assigned by both B. and C. before it became due, no set-off could be made, except of a demand against D.” (Cowen’s Tr. 3d Ed. vol. 2, p. 188, citing Edw. Tr. 8d Ed. 61).

When a negotiable note is indorsed and transferred after it is due, and the defendant relies upon matter of set-off which he may have against the promisee, he can avail himself only of such matter of defense as existed between himself and the promisee at the time of the actual indorsement and transfer of the note to the holder. Notes, or other matters of set-off, acquired by the defendant against the promisee after such transfer, cannot be given in evidence in defense to such note, although the maker had no notice of such transfer at the time of acquiring his demand against the promisee (Baxter v. Little, 6 Mete. 7). “When it is said that the assignment of a negotiable security overdue

§ 258. But the foregoing rule, just and reasonable as it seems, has not been universally observed. 

In New Hampshire, in an action by the indorsee of a negotiable promissory note, who paid a valuable consideration for it, and to whom it was bona fide, transferred shall not deprive a defendant of any considerations which might have been favorable to him, if the action had been brought by the original holder, it is meant that such facts as would show that the security at the time of the assignment had become invalid in the hands of the original holder, should equally avail the defendant against the assignee. But it never could have been intended by the statute that an assignee should be bound to contest a demand made by the defendant against his assignor on a negotiable security which the defendant might have purchased subsequently. This would, in many instances, enable a defendant, by collusion with the assignor, to defeat the effect of an assignment; because the assignee being a stranger to the transaction relied upon in the defense, could have no means of protecting himself” (Sedgwick, J., in Holland v. Makepeace, 8 Mass. 418).

A note to pay $212 in half-yearly instalments is overdue when the first instalment is past due and unpaid, and one to whom it is transferred afterwards takes it subject to all equities between the original parties (Vinton v. King, 4 Allen, 562).

Although a promissory note past due and dishonored, and which has been protested for non-payment, passes by delivery, and an action may be maintained upon it by the holder, subject to the equities of the parties thereto, yet it cannot be said to pass in the usual course of trade and business. The holder takes it in the light of an assignee of a person from whom he receives it, and he, therefore, takes just such title, and no other, as his assignor had to it at the time of the transfer (Farrington v. Park Bank, 89 Barb. 645).

“The declarations or admissions of the payee of a note have been admitted in evidence to defeat a recovery upon the note by one to whom it was indorsed when overdue; but they appear to have been admissions made by the party while he held the note. The principle upon which such evidence has been deemed competent, seems to be that they are admissions in relation to the title to property which the party then held. Any one who may have the legal title. In the other case, he has made no such contract. When a note is negotiable it may be assigned, and the legal title passes to the assignee whether it is discredited or not, and whether the maker has a set-off against the payee or not. When a discredited note has been in reality assigned for a valuable consideration, the debt is due to the assignee; and in a suit upon the note, in the name of the indorsee against the maker, the indorsee and the maker are the real as well as the nominal parties. And the indorsee cannot be considered as standing in the place of the indorser, unless the note can be considered as still due to the indorser; or, the indorsee, by taking the discredited note as having made the set-off his own debt, either of which is repugnant to common sense.” *

* “It is a just and equitable rule that he who takes a discredited note shall take it subject to any legal or equitable defense to which it was liable in the hands of any previous holder. But is a set-off a defense within the meaning of this rule? Strictly speaking, a set-off is not a defense. When the claim of the plaintiff is wholly paid by a set-off, the action is at an end. But his claim has not been defeated by a defense, but has been paid by the extinguishment of claims against him to an equal amount. The question is not whether there should be a set-off in such a case, but whether there can be one under the statute. All mutual demands, equitable as well as legal, between the real parties to the suit, are within the statute. This is the utmost extent of the rule. And, from the very nature of it, nothing can be a set-off but a claim against a person whom the defendant has a right to consider the real plaintiff. Nothing is more common than the transfer of discredited notes. And if there can be a set-off in these cases, it must be of the general balance due to the maker upon an adjustment of all demands between him and the payee. There can be no sound reason why a set-off should be admitted if the maker, on an adjustment of all demands between them, is indebted to the payee in the amount of the note. And if the indorsee is compelled, after having paid the indorser the amount of the note, to litigate all demands and accounts between the maker and the payee, to which he is an entire stranger, and subjected to all the expense of the litigation, if the balance in favor of the maker turns out to be equal to the amount of the note, the case of the indorser may be quite as hard, in some instances, as any that can occur if the set-off be rejected. Besides, if a claim in favor of the maker against the payee, is a legal set-off to a discredited note, a claim in his favor against any other legal holder of the note, through whose hands it may have passed, must be equally so. And this may lead to cases of still greater hardship on the side of an innocent indorsee” (Richardson, C. J., in Chandler v. Drew, supra).

§ 259 — SET-OFF AGAINST PAYEE OF NOTE.

29. Set-off against payee of note, in action by indorsee.

§ 259. The maker of a negotiable promissory note cannot, in an action on the note, by the indorsee, set off a demand against the original payee, unless it be shown that the note was transferred after it was due, or in order to defraud the maker of his set-off. (a)

“When an indorsee takes a bill or note by endorsement before it is due, and without notice of fraud or other matter of defense, he takes it on an independent title by endorsement, and will not be affected by any payment, set-off, fraudulent consideration, or other matter of defense which the acceptor or promiser might have had against any previous holder or prior party. He is not in privity with such prior party, does not claim under him, and is not bound by the acts, frauds, or admissions of any such prior party. And in order to give the highest credit and the freest circulation to negotiable securities transferred by endorsement, in favor of commerce, this principle is held with great firmness and strictness, and by a series of recent decisions, the rule upon the subject, instead of being relaxed, is held with greater strictness than formerly.

“But where a negotiable note is found in circulation after it is due, it carries suspicion on the face of it. The question instantly arises: ‘Why is it in circulation? Why is it not paid?’ Therefore, although it does not give the indorsee notice of any specific matter of defense, such as set-off, payment, or fraudulent acquisition, yet it puts him on inquiry. He takes only such title as the indorser himself has, and subject to any defense which would be made if the suit were brought by the indorser. The

(a) Hendricks agst. Judah, 1 Johns. 819,

This rule is settled by a series of authorities which show not only that such defense may be made, but that it may be proved by the same evidence by which it might have been proved if the indorser were plaintiff, to-wit: the admissions of such indorser made whilst he was the holder.” (a) *

Martin, B., delivering the opinion of the court, said: “The statute enacts that where there are mutual debts between the plaintiff and the defendant, one debt may be set against the other.” This is the whole enactment as applicable to the present case, and upon its true construction the question depends. If the words of the statute had been, that where there were mutual debts the one might be set against the other, the argument for the defendant might have had more weight. But these are not the only words; for the debts are to be mutual debts between the plaintiff and the defendant, and there is no debt here due from the plaintiff at all; and, except the words, between the plaintiff and defendant, can be excluded, the plea cannot be maintained.

The U.S. Federal Courts, so far as they have expressed themselves on the subject, seem to favor such a set-off. In Campbell v. Hamilton, 4 Wash. C. C. R. 92, Washington, J., in delivering the opinion of the U.S. Circuit Court for the third Circuit, remarked that “there were cases in which the courts of common law have taken notice of equitable interests and enforced them; thinking it better to do so in those particular instances than to put the party out of court and send him to another forum. Thus, in an action on a bond given to the plaintiff in trust for another, the defendant will be allowed to set off a debt due from the person beneficially interested, in like manner, as if such person were and could be legally the plaintiff.”

The condition of the bond states that the money belongs to them, and that it is for their use and benefit. This case is, therefore, nothing more nor less than the common one of a debt made payable to A., for the use of B. It comes within the principle above stated, which regards, even at law, the beneficial owner as the real one.”

Stracey v. Deey, 7 Term. R. 861, n., was an action of assumpsit for goods sold, Pleas, non-assumpsit and set-off. The plaintiffs jointly carried on trade as grocers, but Ross was the only ostensible person engaged in the business, and appeared to the world to be solely interested therein. By the terms of the partnership, Ross was to be the apparent trader, and the others were to remain sleeping partners. The defendant was a policy broker, and being indebted for groceries to Ross, he effected insurances and paid premiums on account of Ross, solely to the amount of his debt, under the idea that one demand might be set off against the other. Payment of the money due from the defendant was demanded by the firm and was refused by him, on the ground of his having been deceived by the other partners keeping back. Lord Kenyon, C. J., was of opinion that, as the defendant had a good defense by way of set-off as against Ross, and had been led by the conduct of the plaintiffs to believe that Ross was the only person contracted with, they could not now pull off the mask, and claim payment of debts supposed to be due to Ross alone, without allowing the party the same advantages and equities in his defense that he would have had in actions brought by Ross.

Why is it that when the name of the principal is not disclosed, the law regards the agent in the light of a principal? For the obvious reason that the party contracted with cannot by any probability know that anyone else has an interest in the thing contracted about, and acting upon the belief, it would be unreasonable that he should not have the benefit of anything done in pursuance of it. If, for instance, he has paid money on the faith of such contract, or incurred responsibilities for the agent, or in fine has done any other act which will place him in a worse situation than he would have been in if he had known of the agency, then he will be protected, but not otherwise” (Conyers v. Magrath, supra, Johnson, J.)

But the principal, by suing in his own name, cannot defeat the existing equities between the vendee and the factor, unless they are chargeable with collusion, or there has been some act on the part of the vendee, which operates as a fraud upon the owner of the property. “1st. The purchase may be made by the broker expressly for and in the name of his principal. In that case, if the principal be debited by the seller, he only, and not the broker, will be liable. 2d. A broker may purchase in his character of broker for a known principal; but the seller may choose nevertheless to take him for his debtor, rather than the principal, in whose credit he may not have the same confidence; and after this deliberate election, the seller cannot afterwards turn round and charge the principal. 3d. The broker may buy in his own name, without disclosing his principal, in which case the invoices will of course be made out to him, and he will be debited with the account. If now, before payment, the seller discovers that the purchase was in fact made for another, he may, at his choice, look for payment either to the broker or the principal—to the former upon his personal contract—to the latter upon the contract of his agent; and the adoption of the purchase by the principal will be evidence of the agent’s authority. But, 4th. If after the disclosure of the principal the seller lie by, and suffer the principal to settle in account with his broker for the amount of the purchase, he cannot afterwards charge the latter, so as to make him a loser, but will be deemed to have elected the broker for his debtor. They sold the whole of it accordingly to Kenyon and Son. The latter were likewise brokers, and bought this coffee for the defendants. At the time of the sale, however, Kenyon and Son did not mention that they were purchasers for other persons; and until after they had become bankrupts, it was not known who their principals were. Kymer and M'Tagart had at first entered in their books, “Bought of Waring and Co., sixty-two bags of coffee, d&c., on account of Kenyon and Co.” They then added “For Favenck and Co.” Kenyon and Son, at the time of their bankruptcy, which happened before the sum to be paid for the coffee was due, were indebted to the defendants in a greater amount. Had the credit been originally given to the defendants, paying the price to the servant, if the latter omit to pay it over to the creditor (Paley’s Agency, 245).

The character of a broker is essentially different from that of a factor. A factor is a person to whom goods are consigned for sale by a merchant residing abroad, or at a distance from the place of sale, and he usually sells in his own name without disclosing that of his principal. The latter, therefore, with full knowledge of these circumstances, trusts him with the actual possession of the goods, and gives him authority to sell in his own name. But the broker is in a different situation; he is not entrusted with the possession of the goods, and he ought not to sell in his own name. The principal, therefore, who trusts a broker, has a right to expect that he will not sell in his own name; and if the broker sells without disclosing the name of his principal, he acts beyond the scope of his authority, and the buyer cannot set off a debt due from the broker to him against the demand for the goods made by the principal (Baring et als. v. Corrie et al. 2 Bar. & Ald. 187).

Thus, in an action of assumpsit for money lent, and goods sold and delivered, to which the defendant pleaded the general issue, and gave notice of set-off, it appeared that the articles contained in the set-off were three several sums of money, which were stated to have been paid by the defendant for the plaintiff, and by his direction. On the part of the plaintiff, the allowance of this sum, in the present action, was objected to, on the ground that this was an action by the husband alone, and the debt attempted to be set off was a debt due by the wife before marriage; for which the action should be against husband and wife. But it was answered that the husband having ordered the money to be paid, had thereby made the debt his own. Eyre, C. J., said: “For a debt of the wife dum sola, the action must be against husband and wife, and therefore could not be set off against a claim made by the husband alone, and for which the action was brought. But if it appeared that the husband after the marriage had ordered

the payment of the debt, it would then be a different case.” Therefore, if they are not recovered during the coverture, he is discharged; and if he dies before the debts are collected, his legal representatives are not liable. Mr. Kent (Com. vol. 2, 9th ed. p. 132) remarks, “That the rule of law on this subject may operate very injuriously to creditors; for if the wife be largely indebted before marriage, and the husband takes and appropriates all her personal property to himself, and the wife dies before the creditors have collected their debts, the husband is no longer liable, and the creditors of the wife are left without remedy; and though the wife remains liable, after her husband’s death, for her former debts remaining unpaid, she may have no property to pay them.”

In New York, suits to recover debts contracted by the wife before marriage may be brought against husband and wife; but the judgment and execution affect the separate estate of the wife only. A husband, however, who acquires the separate property of his wife, is liable to the extent of such property for her debts contracted before marriage (Laws of N. Y. of 1858, ch. 576.)

§ 276. The nature and propriety of the requirement under consideration will appear from the following example:—

A debtor gave to his creditor an order on a third person, payable at sight, the amount when received to be placed to the debtor's credit. The creditor, without the knowledge or consent of his debtor took the drawee’s acceptance payable at sixty days, and before the time expired, the acceptor died insolvent. It is manifest that the drawer’s claim against his creditor on account of the draft might be merely nominal, or it might amount to the sum mentioned in the draft. If the drawee was insolvent at the date of the bill, or when it came into the creditor’s hands, or if any other cause rendered it prudent for him to take an acceptance at sixty days, a jury would give no damages, and other circumstances might as to be a proper set-off, the only restriction upon the right is, that the plaintiff's action shall be “founded upon demands which could themselves be the subject of set-off according to law.” Therefore, the joinder by the plaintiff of an unfounded claim for unliquidated damages, in the same suit with other claims which are subject to set-off, will not deprive the defendant of his right to reduce the plaintiff's demand by counter-claim (Smith v. § 277. An unsettled account would constitute a claim not only unliquidated but wholly uncertain.

Upon the foreclosure of a mortgage by the husband, who upon the decease of his wife has become entitled to the benefit thereof, the mortgage having been given to the wife by her guardian after the guardianship had terminated, as security for what he might be found to owe her as guardian upon an accounting, the guardian cannot maintain a cross bill to have his guardian account settled, so that he may set off the balance against the mortgage. Nor can the guardian in such suit, the wife having executed a refunding bond, with sureties, and there having been no final settlement of the estate, set off his ward’s proportion of a judgment which has been rendered against him as executor of her father’s estate. Neither can he set off what is coming to him under an agreement by his ward to pay him for his services as executor of her father’s estate, of which she was a distributee, the law only allowing him such compensation as might be fixed by the Probate Court upon a final settlement of the estate. There is some confusion and apparent conflict in the authorities as to what, in a given case, shall be deemed a penalty, and what liquidated damages. The subject is too extensive to be embraced in a note. What follows will give a good general idea of the understanding of the courts in relation to liquidated damages:

In Watt’s Exr. v. Sheppard, 2 Ala. 425, the court, per Collier, C. J., in an able opinion, deduced from the authorities the following conclusions: 1st, Where the damages which may result from the non-performance of a contract are uncertain, and cannot be admeasured with any degree of accuracy, there the sum agreed to be paid by the party in default will be regarded as liquidated damages. 2d, Where a person stipulates to perform work by a definite time, and upon default, to pay so much weekly or monthly; if the sum is not so unreasonably large as to induce the belief that the parties never contemplated its payment, it will be considered as liquidated damages. And see Mundy v. Culver, 18 Barb. 836.

Where parties to a contract for mutual performance within a given time, respectively bound themselves “each to the other in the sum of $500, for the faithful performance of the several agreements herein entered into,” it was held that the sum specified was liquidated damages (Gammon v. Howe, 14 Maine R. 250).

In Tingley v. Cutler, 7 Conn. 291, the defendant had agreed to purchase an estate of the plaintiff, and to pay therefor at the times and in the manner stipulated. There was a further clause on the back of the agreement signed by the defendant, in these words: “If Elisha Cutler does not perform, according to the within instrument, he shall pay the sum of one hundred and fifty dollars.” This was held to be liquidated damages.

In Reilly v. Jones, 8 Moore’s R. 244, it is said that where it may be fairly collected that the intent of the parties was that the damages stipulated for as between themselves were to be considered as liquidated damages, they cannot be treated as a penalty, although they might operate as such in a popular sense. And see Chamberlain v. Bagley, 11 N. H. R. 234; Brewster v. Edgerly, 18 N. H. 275; Mead v. Wheeler, Ib. 351.

“Where the parties plainly say and mean that a certain sum of money shall be paid if a certain thing be done, or be omitted to be done, the only objection to enforcing the payment arises from its assumed inequity. But before we act upon that reason, we must satisfy ourselves, if indeed that be possible, that we thoroughly understand what would be equitable between the parties to the suit” (Gilchrist, J., in Mead v. Wheeler, supra).

Where there was a stipulation in a building contract that the building should be completed by a certain day, and in default thereof a deduction of $100 for every month which intervened between that day and the finishing of the house, it was held that the forfeiture took the character of liquidated damages (Worrell v. M’Clinaghan, 5 Strobh. 115).

“Where there is a manifest difficulty in ascertaining damages arising from the breach of the contract, and the fair conclusion is that the amount is specified and agreed on for the purpose of saving the expense or avoiding the difficulty of proving the actual damages, the parties should be held to their bargain; and especially where the amount fixed and liquidated is not

* But we shall see hereafter, that the defendant may set up such damages by way of recoupment.

The New York revised statutes curtailed set-off as previously allowed. By the revised laws (1 R. L. 515) it existed in all cases where two or more persons dealing together were indebted to each other, or had demands arising on contract or credits against each other. That was general, and related to demands upon contracts generally. Now set-offs are limited to contracts of certain descriptions, and if they are not such, then the amount must be liquidated, or capable of being ascertained by calculation.

The New York Revised Statutes (5th ed vol. 3, p. 635) specify the cases in which set-offs may be allowed, as follows: “It must be a demand for real estate sold, or for personal property sold, or for money paid or services done; or if it be not such a demand, the amount must be liquidated or be capable of being ascertained by calculation.”

“On a hearing in damages, the Court will not offset mutual covenants in a deed” (Cochran v. Leister, 2 Root, 848).

It is supposed that the case, in 2 Schoals & Lefry, 408, note, is an authority in conflict with the general doctrine so strongly laid down by Chancellor Kent in 8 Johns Ch. R. 358; Ib. 575-576; 4 Ib. 287; and by Chancellor Walworth in 8th Paige Rep. 597, that there is no case to be found where uncertain damages have been set off growing out of a breach of covenant, there being no express or implied agreement in the transaction, and no special cause shown. But in that very case, the arbitrators by their award ascertained the unliquidated damages. And so Judge Story treats this exceptional case in discussing this subject (Lumpkin, J., in Bonaud v. Sortel, 21 Geo. R. 108).

It is now settled that the dependency or independency of mutual covenants does not arise from the use of any particular phraseology, such as covenant, condition, consideration or the like, or on the collocation of words and sentences in an instrument. The nature of the transaction, and the object and design of the parties are to be looked at, and such construction is to be given as will best effectuate their object and do justice between them (right v. Smyth, 4 Watts & Serg. 527). If the action be brought for a demand which is unliquidated, it falls within the rule which requires that the claim of the plaintiff shall be such as might itself be the subject of set-off. Therefore, in an action of debt on a bond conditioned for the performance
