10. Unliquidated claim for loss upon open policy of insurance.

§ 292. An unliquidated claim for loss upon an open policy of insurance cannot be set off in a suit at law brought against the assured by the underwriters for the recovery of a debt due from the former to the latter. 

The damages to be recovered on a policy of insurance are always uncertain; the amount depends on the proof at the trial. The plaintiff may declare for a total loss, yet be able to prove only a partial loss, the extent of which will be greater or less according to the circumstances of each particular case. A policy of insurance is a contract of indemnity. The assurer undertakes to indemnify the assured for the damages he may sustain by losses in consequence of the perils insured against by the policy. It is like a bond to save harmless. In most cases nothing can be more unliquidated than the amount of such indemnity. It depends upon a great variety of facts and circumstances to be disclosed and digested at the trial.

* In Indiana, it seems to have been held that a defendant, who was a member of a firm which has been dissolved, may set off an unliquidated demand growing out of the unsettled partnership accounts.

In Irish v. Snelson, 16 Ind. R. 365, A., B. and C. brought an action against D. on a promissory note payable to E., who assigned it to the plaintiffs. The note was made in 1857. It appeared that the defendant and E., the payee of the note, in 1853 and until March, 1858, were copartners, when the copartnership was dissolved by mutual consent. It was claimed by the defendant that upon the dissolution of the firm, E. was indebted to him on partnership account, and that said indebtedness accrued to him before notice of the assignment of the note to the plaintiffs, and he now offered to set off said indebtedness against the sum due the plaintiffs on the note. It was held that the set-off was proper.

Davidson, J., in delivering the opinion of the court, said: “The demand in this instance proposed as a set-off could not have been allowed as such anterior to the present code, because, until a final settlement of the partnership accounts, one partner could not maintain an action against his co-partner for money advanced on account of the partnership. And upon the same principle, an unliquidated and unsettled partnership demand would not have been allowed as a set-off. But the statutory rule now is, that the defendant may set forth in his answer as many grounds of defense, counterclaim and set-off, whether legal or equitable, as he shall have (2 "Rey. Sts. of Indiana, p. 89, § 56). And a set-off, as defined by the same statute, must consist of matter arising out of a debt, duty or contract, liquidated or not, held by the defendant at the time the suit was commenced, and matured at or before the time it is offered as a set-off (Ibid. § 57). As we construe these enactments, an equitable demand arising out of contract, though unliquidated, may be the subject of set-off. And the answer in question must be sustained because the matter which it proposes to set off arises out of a contract of partnership. The business operations of the firm, it is true, are unsettled, and the demand was consequently unliquidated. But the partnership having been dissolved, the demand existed in its unliquidated form.

The defendant therefore demanded that an account of the partnership concerns be taken, and that such sum as should be found to be justly due to the defendant should be set off in this action. Held, on demurrer, that the answer showed no counter-claim against the plaintiff arising out of a cause of action on contract existing at the commencement of the suit. (a)*

The answer did not allege that the plaintiff owed the firm, or that anything would be due from the plaintiff to the defendant on the first winding up of the copartnership concerns. But held that if it had contained such an allegation, it would still have been insufficient” (Ives v. Miller, supra, per and, P. J., disapproving Gage v. Angell, 8 How. Pr. R. 335).

“One partner has no demand, debt or counter-claim against his copartner before or after dissolution until a final settlement, where there is no fraud, nor an express agreement, nor any special circumstances” (Ib).

“Each partner has a specific lien on the partnership effects, not only for the amount of his share but for moneys advanced by him for the use of the firm beyond his share, and for money abstracted by a copartner beyond his share. Upon dissolution each party may insist upon a sale of the property. The funds and other assets are to be collected, an account taken, and all the creditors ascertained and paid. On the final accounting each partner is to be allowed, as against the other, what he has brought into the business, and may charge his copartner with what the latter has not but should have brought in, and with what he has taken out beyond his proportionate share, and nothing is to be considered his share but his proportion of the residue or balance of the account” (Ib. and cases cited).

§ 298. Damages arising from the negligence of the plaintiff in a different transaction cannot be set off.*

It has somewhere been justly remarked, that the statutes of set-off never intended that a plaintiff should be surprised by such demands in answer to his action upon a promissory note or bill of exchange, or for goods.

* But where they arise from negligence in the same transaction they may be recouped.

This provision gave to the defendant H. a right to one-half the amount of the charges in the book, for fulling and carding work done by the plaintiff, under the obligation that the defendant should collect that half himself. To do so, it was indispensably necessary that he should have access to the books, to take copies of his share of the accounts in them, in order to receive and collect them, with a right to the production of the books by the plaintiff when requisite to substantiate the claim. Without this, his right to the one-half the moneys due as rent, would be nugatory. Or, at any rate, the plaintiff should have furnished him correct transcripts of his share of the accounts, if he would not permit the defendant to make them himself. The plaintiff’s refusing both, was doing the defendant an injury commensurate with the amount which the defendant lost by the refusal. It is true the damages are unliquidated; but there is

§ 312. Demands remain mutual after verdict the same that they did before. The verdict does not annihilate or extinguish the debt, nor change the nature of it, or the rule of law. It only amounts to conclusive evidence of the debt; so that the same right of set-off continues to exist. (a)*

In Massachusetts, the statute (Rev. Laws, ch. 167, § 19) provides that "Whenever a judgment is rendered in one action, and the same parties are defendants in another action in which the plaintiffs are the same, the court may, on application, set off one judgment against the other, and the balance due may be collected in the same action."

In New Jersey, the statute (Rev. Stat. 1937, § 3:18-1) states that “If judgments are rendered in actions against parties in the same right, the court may order the judgments to be set off against each other and that execution shall issue for the balance only.”

In New York, the statute (C.L. § 274) establishes that “Mutual judgments may be set off against each other in the same action, as often as may be necessary to determine the rights of the respective parties, provided the demands are mutual and of the same nature.”

In Pennsylvania, the Common Pleas rules allow for set-offs in actions where the judgments can be mutual and their enforcement sought through the same court.

In South Carolina, the statute (Code of Laws, § 19-83) permits the court to set off any judgment against another if the parties are the same and the demands are mutual.

In Virginia, the statute (Code of Virginia, § 8.01-271) states that judgments may be set off whenever the same parties are involved in mutual judgments rendered either in the same or different courts.

In West Virginia, the law (W. Va. Code § 56-1-2) allows for set-offs in cases where the parties are the same and the claims are mutual.

In summary, many states provide mechanisms allowing for the set-off of judgments when the same parties are involved in mutual debts or claims, thus facilitating the resolution of conflicting judgments.

Some of the adjudged cases go upon the principle of extending the statutes of set-off in their spirit of equity and justice. The law of set-off, before judgment, is regulated entirely by statute. When the mutual claims of parties have passed into judgments, it is the practice of the courts to set off one judgment against the other. This practice does not rest upon any statute, but upon the general jurisdiction of courts over the suitors in them” (Richardson, C. J., in Chandler v. Drew, supra).

The power to set one judgment against another is an inherent one, and the only equitable power which the common law courts originally possessed” (Burns v. Thornburgh, supra).

Applications of this kind, which are founded on no positive statute or any fixed rule which compels the court to grant them, are addressed to the discretion of the court; and in the exercise of that discretion, even though the set-off might legally be made, yet if the court sees that injustice will be done by granting the order of set-off, it is uniformly refused (Tolbert v. Whether a set-off shall be allowed in a given case “is indeed a matter resting in discretion; but this means judicial discretion, regulated by the principles of equity and justice; not a wanton, capricious, or arbitrary determination of the will” (Platt, J., in Simpson v. Hart, 14 Johns. 63).

It has been justly remarked that “the exercise of this power by courts is productive of equitable results, by affording a speedy and inexpensive mode of the settlement of counter-claims between litigants, and should not be unnecessarily restricted” (Flandrau, J., in Temple v. Scott, supra).

In Simpson v. Hart, 14 Johns. R. 63, the plaintiff had made an application to the mayor's court of the City of New York for a set-off of judgments, which was denied, and the question before the court of errors was whether the chancellor was bound to disregard the decision of the mayor's court and to re-examine and decide upon the merits of the complainant’s bill, as if the relief had been originally sought in his court. The majority of the court held that he was, and that the proceedings should be remitted to the court of chancery, in order that the set-off might be allowed. Platt, J., dissenting, contended that the motion for set-off rested on the same footing as a motion for a new trial, and one court having, in the exercise of its discretion, denied the set-off, it could not be granted by another court. A principal ground for the allowance of the set-off in this case was, however, newly discovered evidence.

But if the debtor abandons the pursuit of the property itself, and relies upon recovering its value, he cannot claim for the representative of that value, whether it be in money, notes, or a judgment, any higher character than property of the same class is entitled to, under ordinary circumstances.”

§ 330. The defendant must have obtained the judgment under such circumstances as to have a clear right to enforce it.

The decision in the following case turned upon the circumstance that the transaction being the purchase of the subject matter of a suit by the attorney, it was void as against the policy of the law.

The plaintiff obtained a verdict for £50 against the defendant, in an action in which all the proceedings, down to final judgment, were carried on in the name of A., as attorney for the plaintiff, and judgment was signed in that action for £85 damages and costs in March, 1855. A few days before the trial, B. entered into an arrangement with A. that he should have the conduct of the suit as the plaintiff's attorney, A’s name being still continued on the record until February, 1856, when B.’s name was substituted. On the day after the trial, B., at the request of the plaintiff who was in want of money, purchased the verdict for the sum of £50, and gave notice of his claim to the defendant’s attorney, and requested that the damages recovered should be paid only to himself or A. In July, 1855, the plaintiff was non-suited in another action against the same defendant, and judgment of non-suit for £71 costs was signed in that action in January, 1856. Held, that the defendant was, under the circumstances, entitled to set off his judgment for £71 against that for £85 recovered by the

§ 331. Where different interests are involved, or one of the parties may be injuriously affected by a decision on the merits of the motion; as where it is shown that persons besides the nominal creditor are interested as legatees or assignees, in the demand on which one of

* In Simpson v. Lamb, supra, it was held, that it made no difference that the purchaser was not attorney on the record. Semble, that such a purchase by a stranger to the suit, would have been valid. In that case, Campbell, C. J., said: “The purchase of the damages immediately after the verdict and before judgment, was a purchase of the matter in suit pendente lite, and it may be very material to consider in what relation Shaen stood to the plaintiff at the time of the purchase. It appears that although Scott was nominally the attorney for the plaintiffs, down to a time long subsequent to the final judgment, Shaen became, before the trial, really and substantially the attorney for the plaintiffs in the management and conduct of the suit; and it appears to us, that for the purpose of the question before us, Shaen is to be considered as the attorney having the management of the cause for the plaintiffs, and that the purchase was in effect a purchase by the attorney in the cause of the subject matter of it, pendente lite, not for the purpose of enabling them to carry on the suit, but because they wanted the money. Independently of the statutes referred to, upon the arguments restraining the purchase of property in suits, particularly by persons concerned in the administration of justice, it has been held in several cases that no attorney can be permitted to purchase anything in litigation, of which litigation he has the management; and, considering the situation in which the attorney and client stand to each other, it would seem to be against the policy of the law to permit such a dealing by an attorney with the subject of a suit of which he has the conduct as attorney, while the case is still undetermined by judgment, as that which is now in question before us, whatever might have been the case had the purchase been by a stranger.”

It is the policy of the law to scrutinize gifts, conveyances and securities, given by a client to his attorney pending the relation, more especially when they are connected with the subject matter of litigation; as then the necessities of the client and the confidence reposed, place the client most in the power of his attorney. The relation and confidence it implies, which confidence is absolutely necessary, in some cases, to promote the prosecution or defense of a suit, are frequently not so much a matter of choice with the client as of necessity. Hence, the reason and justice of the rule of law that will not permit them to be turned to the profit of the attorney at the expense of the client (Gray v. Emmons, 7 Mich. 533).

Tolbert v. Harrison, () was a rule upon the plaintiff to show cause why a judgment recovered against him in another action by the defendant in this case, should not be set off against the present judgment. It was objected that the debts were not in the same right. The defendant's judgment was upon the individual contract of the plaintiff. The plaintiff’s judgment was upon a note payable to “Joseph Tolbert, executor of John Tolbert.” In the pleadings, the plaintiff described himself as executor, and the note was set forth as payable in that character. It was proved that the note was given for goods of the testator, bought by the defendant at the executor’s sale; and it was further alleged that the executor had no other assets of his testator in his hands to pay debts, and which, therefore, could not be paid without resorting to property in which the widow had a life estate under the will.

The court, per O’Neale, J., said: “There can be no doubt that technically the judgments are in the same right. The note given to the executor for a contract made with him, must be treated and considered as his own. In a legal point of view, it was the note of Sterling Harrison to Joseph S. Tolbert. It is, however, unquestionable, that in fact, it was a part of the assets of the estate of his testator, and the executor might, and ought to have treated it as such. He, on the present occasion, claims that it should be considered as the assets of the estate. This is the equity of the case; and a court of equity in the exercise of the jurisdiction

§ 333 MUST BE IN THE SAME RIGHT.

which legitimately belongs to it over trustees, will follow a note of hand, as the property of an estate, if really taken for assets of the estate sold by the administrator, though the note be taken in the private name of the administrator, and will enforce this, by injunction against the private creditors of the administrator. The question is, whether this court is bound by legal rules, to set off judgments in all cases where they are in the same right. It is clear that it is not. All applications of this kind, founded as they are on no positive statute, or any fixed rule which compels the court to grant them, are addressed to the discretion of the court; and in the exercise of that discretion, even where the set-off might be legally made, if the court sees that injustice will be done by granting the order of set-off, it is uniformly refused. In this case, positive injustice would be done, not to the parties before the court, but to the estate of the testator. The note justly belongs to that estate. If the court of law had granted the application, the court of equity, at the instance of the tenant for life, under the will of the testator, would have enjoined the proceedings.

The revised statutes of Massachusetts, ch. 90, § 50, provide for the setting off of cross judgments under the direction of the court, and enact that if there are several defendants, each of them may bring a cross action against the original plaintiff, and on recovering judgment may be allowed to set off such several judgment against the plaintiff’s judgment in like manner as if against himself alone.

In Connecticut, the statute provides that in all actions of trespass other than actions of assault and battery, and other than such as are brought for damages for the taking of property exempt from execution, and in all actions of trespass on the case in which judgment is rendered in favor of the plaintiff, the defendant or defendants may set off against such judgment any debt which he or they may hold, either jointly or severally, against the plaintiff, excepting that no debt acquired by the defendant after the accruing of the cause of action upon which such judgment was rendered can be set off. In such case, a bill in equity must be filed in the court where the judgment was rendered within twenty-four hours after final judgment and before the rising of the court, praying for such set-off. If defendant's claim is admitted by the plaintiff, the court proceeds forthwith to make the set-off. But if the demand of the defendant is denied by the plaintiff, the set off will not be allowed, unless the defendant, previous to the rendition of the judgment in favor of the plaintiff, instituted a suit upon such demand. In case such suit is pending at the time of the rendition of such judgment, the court will order a stay of execution thereon, and if the defendant recovers judgment, one judgment will be set off against the other (Sts. of Conn. ed. of 1866, pp. 24, 25).

The court, per Gibson, J., said:

“The objection to the set-off is that the defendant acquired whatever equitable interest he now has in his judgment after the plaintiff had assigned his interest in his verdicts to his counsel, who, being the real parties in interest, ought not, it is said, to be affected by any act or change of the original parties after the interest had vested under the assignment from the plaintiff. It is certain the equitable is the substantial interest in a suit; and as it constitutes the real ownership of the right to be recovered, it will be treated accordingly. It would, therefore, have been immaterial that the defendant all along remained the legal owner of the judgment he had assigned if the equitable ownership had been entirely divested and re-acquired after other parties had obtained such an interest in the opposite demand as the law would protect. But, by the assignment of the defendant, this judgment passed not absolutely but on particular trusts; and consequently, there was a resulting trust to the assignor, which in such cases always remains to him. After the particular trusts were either executed or withdrawn by the assignor and the trustees, the old interest re-vested, or rather was revived in the party just as if it had never been out of him or modified by his acts. In truth, an assignment of this kind by which the legal interest is unchanged, and only a portion of the equitable interest parted with, and that, too, only for a special purpose, more resembles an assignment for collateral security than a conveyance of the right, and is to be esteemed such only by those who are parties to it. For, after the rights of those beneficially interested are withdrawn, it does not lie with third persons to say the property was ever divested. The defendant had a right to redeem his judgment by paying his creditors or satisfying them in any other way.

<br>

In an early case in Pennsylvania, the court seemed to have laid some stress on the fact that the set-off was not offered at the trial. It said: “On the question ‘whether the defendant shall now be permitted to set off this assigned judgment, it is material to consider that he had it in his power to offer it on the trial of the cause; that he gave notice of his intention to do it, but that for some reason it was not done. In the trial before the jury or referees, it would have been highly proper to claim the benefit of a set-off, which, having been then waived by the defendant, he comes now with a very ill grace to ask it of this court. It certainly diminishes the equity of his application, if he ever had any, and removes every idea of hardship in his being precluded from doing it at this time” (Dunkin v. Calbraith, 1 Browne, 47).

It was formerly supposed that the courts had no authority to grant a rule in cross actions for deducting the costs of one action from those of the other; for the reason that it required a statute to enable the defendant in an action to set off a mutual debt, and that the statute of set-offs did not extend to the case of costs. But the power of directing the costs of cross actions to be set against each other does not depend upon the statute of set-off, but on the general discretionary power of the courts over their suitors (Bright on costs, 302).

Where a creditor’s bill contained only general averments, without any allegation as to any specific property or assets, and it was dismissed, no property of the debtor having been discovered, a motion to set off the costs of dismissal against the judgment was denied (Evans v. Vance, 2 Barb. 598). Edmonds, J., said: “We are determined, in cases like this, which is a mere fishing bill, not founded upon any specific allegation, and not even upon any knowledge or belief that the defendant had any property, not to allow the costs consequent upon the dismissal of the bill to set off against the judgment. Such suits are mostly mere matters of speculation, where the plaintiff indulges in very general charges, and puts very general inquiries, in the expectation that if he fails in finding anything it will cost him nothing, because he can use his judgment against an insolvent debtor, to ward off his liability for the expenses to which he has put his adversary. The effect of this is to encumber this court with useless suits, to use its process and powers for vexatious purposes, and to compel the Supreme Court, on its equity side, to become a most expensive and dilatory instrument of collecting debts. Creditors’ bills are frequently a very valuable aid in the collection of demands against fraudulent debtors; and in that aspect they are deserving the protection of the court. But it is an abuse of their legitimate character when thus resorted to for mere fishing purposes; and we cannot encourage that abuse by allowing the set-off in such cases.”

The proper remedy of the defendant, in case the complainant neglects or refuses to pay the costs, after they have been taxed and demanded, is to proceed as for a contempt. Or, he may consider the suit as still pending,

* The New York Code, § 303, provides that hereafter the measure of the compensation of the attorney shall be left to the agreement, express or implied, of the parties. + In Benedict v. Stuart, 28 Barb, 420, the plaintiff and his partner M. being practising attorneys of New York, entered into a contract with the defendant, who had a cause of action against the New York Central Railroad Company for a personal injury sustained by him as a passenger, by reason of a collision on said road; by which agreement, the plaintiff and M. were to commence and prosecute an action in favor of the defendant against said railroad company, for such cause of action; for which services the defendant should pay or secure them fifty dollars to begin with, and they to have the taxable costs, and twenty percent of the amount recovered in said action. Held, that such agreement was, under the code, lawful. The New York Code leaves the attorney and client to make their own agreement, and, in the absence of proof of an express agreement, it is implied from the nature and value of the services rendered (Easton v. Smith, 61 N. Y. Smith, 818; Stow v. Hamlin, 11 Howard, 452; Wilde v. Joel, 15 N. Y. 820).

In the State of New York, the lien of the attorney upon the judgment for his costs was recognized at an early period. The amount which an attorney might claim for his services, or which might be allowed for such services by the court, was made a matter of statute regulation by an act passed the 18th of February, 1789; although there had been colonial statutes upon the subject as early as 1710. The code has not affected this lien (Ward v. Wordsworth, 1 E. D. Smith, 598).

In Rooney v. Second Avenue Railroad Co., 18 N. Y. R. 368, in the New York Court of Appeals, the question to be determined was whether the code had done away with the attorney’s lien; and it was held that it had not. Harris, J., in delivering the opinion of the court, in which all the judges concurred, said: “The principle upon which the right has been sustained is certainly unaffected by the code. As in other cases of lien, the attorney is protected, because it is by his labor and skill that the judgment has been recovered. The judgment being under the control of the court and the parties within its jurisdiction, it will see that no injustice is done to its own officers. There is no less reason for the exercise of this power now than before the adoption of the code.”

But the lien will be lost by the assignment of the attorney's claim, and will not be revived by a subsequent purchase of the judgment by the attorney (Chappell v. Dann, 21 Barb. 17).

The New York Superior Court held in a recent case that, “although on motions to set off judgments, courts can protect their officers by refusing to set them off, yet that the New York statute of set-offs overrides the lien of the attorney. This reduces the attorney’s lien to something less tenacious than a pledge or common law lien; in fact, makes it a mere claim on the favor of the court. In some cases it has been said that he trusts to the responsibility of his client, and his right must be subordinate to the equities of the parties” (De Figanicre v. Young, 2 Robertson, 670, citing Nicoll v. Nicoll, 16 Wend. 446; Roberts v. Carter, 24 How. Pr. R. 44;

Where the defendant agreed with his attorneys that they should have the costs of the suit for their services in carrying it on, and subsequently assigned to them a judgment in his favor for costs, it was held that the plaintiff in this suit, who, before the assignment, had obtained a judgment against the defendant, could not set

An attorney, by not taking an assignment of the costs to accrue before their recovery, loses the right of availing himself of a strict construction of the statutes of set-off of New York, which are confined to cases of contract reduced to judgment, and do not reach costs or damages on a contract or tort not yet reduced to judgment (Ibid, citing 2 N. Y. Rev. Sts. 354, § 82; Ib. 174, § 40; Robinson v. Weeks, 6 How. Pr. R. 161; Countryman v. Boyer, 8 Ib. 386; Nash v. Hamilton, 3 Abb. Pr. R. 85).

In Creighton v. Ingersoll, 20 Barb. 541, which was an action for a partition, after the plaintiff’s attorney had become entitled to certain fees for his services and for disbursements, the plaintiffs assigned their shares. Held, that the lien of the attorney was not divested by the assignment. Mitchell, P. J., delivering the opinion of the court, said: “It would be supposing both the assignor and assignees were intending a fraud, to suppose that they meant to assign costs to which the attorney was entitled. Under the old system, the fee bill would be the standard of his compensation, so far as it provided for specific services. Under the code, the party and his attorney are not restricted to that rule of compensation, but may show any other agreed upon between them. It may be more or less than the adjustable costs; and whichever it be, the attorney is entitled to some compensation; and nothing in the code professes to repeal the system under which the lawyer had a lien on the costs for his payment. The fund is in court, and the court can and ought to hold it for the benefit of the one equitably entitled to it. And as no one can have a more equitable title than the one by whose exertions the whole fund was created, the court should see that he is paid before anyone else carries away the fund.”

In Rooney v. Second Avenue R. R. Co. 18 N. Y. R. 868, Comstock, J., in delivering the opinion of the New York Court of Appeals, said: “Section 303 of the code abrogates all rules and provisions of law which might restrain an attorney in agreeing with his client for the measure or mode of his compensation; and it leaves such compensation to the agreement of the parties, express or implied. What was before, not only illegal but disreputable, is now lawful, if not respectable.”

CHAPTER IX.

SET-OFF IN EQUITY.

Origin.

General jurisdiction of the court. Prerequisites.

In the case of the foreclosure of a mortgage. In cases of insolvency.

After appointment of receiver.

Where there is a remedy at law.

Where relief cannot be obtained at law.

Concurrent jurisdiction.

Burden of proof on party making the set-off. The court restricted to the issue.

* As the general rules of set-off are the same in equity as at law, only a few leading topics will be treated in this chapter.

In Elder v. Lasswell, 2 Blackf. 349, the court remarked, that the distinction relied on by the complainant between courts of law and equity on the subject of set-off, did not exist; that the rule was the same in both courts.

“It may be laid down as an established proposition, that a court of equity follows the same general rules as a court of law in relation to set-off. The statutes concerning set-off and reference are remedial; but confer no power on the court to relax the general rules of law” (Woodworth, J., in Van Beuren v. Van Gaasbeck, 4 Cowen, 496, and see Duncan v. Lyon, 3 John. Ch. R. 851).

That courts of law and equity follow the same general doctrines on the subject of set-off, appears from the opinion of Sir Thomas Clarke, in Whitaker v. Rush, Amb. 407. The cases of ex parte Stephens and ex parte Hanson, 11 Ves. 24; 12 Ves. 346, only established, that, under certain circumstances, there may be a set-off in equity, when there can be none at law. Until the statute of 2 Geo. 2, courts of equity followed the rule of law and would not allow mutual unconnected debts to be set off. “If they had done otherwise,” said Lord Mansfield, in Green v. Farmer, 4 Burr. 2214, “they would have stopped the course of law in all cases where there was a mutual demand.” Lord Hardwicke (1 Atk. 287) remarked, that he did not know that a court of equity had gone further than the courts of law in cases of set-off.

It should be observed, however, that although equity generally follows the law as to set-off, yet, that it is with limitations and restrictions. “If there is no connection between the demands, then the rule is at law. But if there is a connection between them, equity acts upon it, and allows a set-off under particular circumstances” (Snell’s Eq. 415).

§ 369 ORIGIN.

1. Origin.

§ 368. The equitable right of set-off is not derived from, or dependent upon, any statutory right, but is founded on the Roman law. (a) *

§ 369. The English chancery judges frequently asserted the doctrine of stoppage, which was known to the equity courts anterior to the statutes of set-off and bankruptcy. +

(a) Freeman v. Lomas, 9 Hare, 109.

* For an outline of the doctrine of the civil law in relation to set-off, see ante, § 8, et seq.

+ It has been said that before the statutes of set-off at law, and the statutes of mutual debts and credits in bankruptcy, courts of equity were in possession of the doctrine of set-off, and acted upon it as grounded upon principles of natural equity; that now, when the court does not find a natural equity going beyond the statutes, the construction is the same in equity as at law; and that the English bankrupt act, enabling the party to prove the balance of an account upon mutual credit, went much further than the party could have gone either in law or equity before, as to set-off.

There can be no doubt that in England, questions as to the rights of debtors and creditors in cases of cross demands between them, arose and were determined in equity, before the right of set-off was introduced into the statute law of that country. There are cases anterior to the statute of 4 Anne, ch. 17, by which the first statutory provision for set-off in bankruptcy was introduced; and there are other cases in equity not falling within the provisions of the statute of Anne between the date of that statute and the statute of 2 Geo. 2d, ch. 22, by which the right of set-off at law was given. It is clear, therefore, that the rights of debtors and creditors in cases of cross demands between them, as those rights subsisted in equity, were not derived from any statutory right of set-off; and, on the other hand, it seems not to be improbable, that the statutory rights were founded on the equitable rule.

Courts of equity did not antecedently to the statutes of set-off exercise any jurisdiction as to set-off, unless some peculiar equity intervened independently of the mere fact of mutual unconnected accounts. Independently of the statutes of set-off, courts of equity in virtue of their general jurisdiction are accustomed to grant relief in all cases, where, although there are mutual and independent debts, yet there is a mutual credit between the parties, founded at the time, upon the existence of some debts due by the crediting party to the other. A court of equity would not hesitate to do so, upon the ground either of the presumed intention of the parties, or of what is called a natural equity. If in such a case, there should be an express agreement to set off the debts against each other pro tanto, there could be no doubt that a court of equity would enforce a specific performance of

§ 377. In a proper case, a court of equity would, by virtue of its general jurisdiction, apply the doctrine of set-off independently of a statute which provided that in suits in chancery for the payment of money, set-offs should be allowed in the same manner and with the like effect as in actions at law. § 378. Where there are cross demands between two parties, of such a nature that if both were recoverable at law they would be the subject of legal set-off, then, if either of the demands is matter of equitable jurisdiction, the set-off will be enforced in equity. (b)

§ 379. But the mere existence of mutual and independent demands does not authorize the interposition of equity to set them off against each other. To warrant the interference of equity, there must be circumstances from which it can be inferred that one debt was incurred under such conditions that it would be unjust to enforce it without allowing a credit for the other. In respect to set-offs upon the naked equity of distinct and unconnected debts, and independently of any statutable regulations, remarks that “It is not very easy to ascertain the exact nature and limits of this jurisdiction from the English authorities. The conclusion which seems deducible from the general current of the English decisions (though most of them have arisen in bankruptcy) is, that courts of equity will set off distinct debts, where there has been a mutual credit, upon the principles of natural justice, to avoid circuity of suits, following the doctrine of compensation of the civil law to a limited extent. That law went further than ours, deeming the debts suo jure set off or extinguished pro tanto; whereas, our law gives the party an election to set off, if he chooses to exercise it; but, if he does not, the debt is left in full force to be recovered in an adversary suit. Since the statutes of set-off of mutual debts and credits, courts of equity have generally followed the course adopted in the construction of the statutes by courts of law; and have applied the doctrine to equitable debts. They have rarely, if ever, broken in upon the decisions at law, unless some other equity intervened which justified them in granting relief beyond the rules of law. And, on the other hand, courts of law sometimes set off equitable against legal debts. The American courts have generally adopted the same principles, as far as the statutes of set-off of the respective States have enabled them to act.”

§ 380. The voluntary payment by the defendant of the debts of the complainant, would not ordinarily entitle the defendant to set off such payment.

D. set up in his answer that he purchased the interest of S., the complainant, in a mill owned jointly by H. and S., for $1,600; that he paid down $450, a note and mortgage for $750, and his bond conditioned to pay

(a) Simmons v. Williams, 27 Ala. 507; Jordan v. Jordan, 12 Geo. R. 77.

* “There may be an equity in allowing unconnected demands to be set off against each other where they are both subsisting at the same time and one has been assigned. But it is by no means so clear an equity as necessarily to justify an enlarged construction of a statute” (Story, J., in Greene v. Darling, 5 Mason R. 201).

Independently of statute, “the mere existence of distinct debts, without mutual credits, or some supervening equity, has never been supposed to give the right of set-off in a court of equity. The general principle has always prevailed, both at law and in equity, that where there were connected accounts of debt and credit, the balance of the accounts constituted the amount due, and was the sum only recoverable” (Holcombes Intr. 265). In the construction of the statutes of set-off, courts of equity have generally followed courts of law, and have applied the doctrine to equitable debts; “but they have rarely broken in upon the decisions at law, unless some other equity intervened, which justified them in granting extraordinary relief.” It has, however, been laid down generally, that wherever the court finds a case of natural equity not within the statute, it will permit an equitable set-off, if, from the nature of the claim, or from the situation of the parties, or by reason of the fraud of one of them, it is impossible to obtain justice in a cross action (Holt’s Bankrupt L, 224).

It sometimes happens that where there are mutual demands between the parties, a court of equity, provided they are such as cannot be made the subject of set-off at law, will interpose between the parties upon equitable principles, and determine the balance. In the same way, a court of bankruptcy, which exercises an equitable as well as legal jurisdiction, will in those cases which do not come strictly within the statute of mutual credit, arrange the account between the parties upon the principle of natural equity. Where, however, the court does not find a natural equity going beyond the statute, the construction of the statute is the same in equity as at law (Henley’s Bankrupt L, 204).

§ 381. A debt cannot be set off in equity any more than at law, unless it existed against the plaintiff, in favor of the defendant, at the time of the commencement of the suit, and had then become due and payable. And to avail himself of the set-off, the defendant must appear and defend the suit and plead or give notice of such set-off, so as to enable the adverse party to bring witnesses to contest the claim.*

§ 382. The debts must be mutual, and exist between the parties in their own right. There is no such thing as an inherent quality or right of set-off in the creation of a debt or demand. It can only arise or attach when there is a mutuality of the debts of such a certain and ascertained character as to be capable of set-off, or of being applied in compensation of each other. (a)

A single example under this head will suffice. Rent due cannot be set off in equity for a breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment. As one demand is for an account of transactions under the contract, and the other

§ 383. Nor will courts of equity any more than courts of law, in general, allow a set-off of a joint debt against a separate debt, or conversely of a separate debt against a joint debt.

It was accordingly held in Holbrook v. Receivers of Am. Fire Ins. Co. that Holbrook’s individual demand for a loss upon a policy of insurance could not be allowed to compensate or satisfy a joint bond of his and another person, which was held by the receivers of the insolvent insurance company, with whom he had effected the insurance; the giving of the bond and the policy of insurance, having no connection as parts of the same transaction, and it not being pretended that the bond was given for the individual debt of Holbrook with the other person as surety only.

In Dale v. Cooke, 4 Johns, Ch. R. 11, Kent, Chancellor, said: “My conclusion is, that joint and separate debts cannot be set off in equity any more than at law; and if the bill were free from other fatal imperfections, and the case reduced to this single point, I should be obliged to deny the motion.” And see the remarks of Judge Story to the same effect, in Howe v. Sheppard, 2 Sumner, 409.

“As the rule of law and in equity is the same, that the right of set-off must be reciprocal, and that mutual claims and such as are in the same right can alone be set off, it follows, that if the proof shows the existence of a claim against two parties, it cannot be set off against the individual claim of one of those parties for the want of that mutuality which the rule requires” (The Chancellor, in Robertson v. Parks, 8 Md. Ch. Decis. 65).

“The general rule,” says Judge Story, in Greene v. Darling, 5 Mason R. 201, “in equity, is like that at law, that there can be no set-off of joint debts against separate debts, unless some new equity justify it. Such an equity may arise under circumstances of fraud; or, where the party seeking relief is only a surety for a debt really separate; or, where there is a series of transactions in which joint credit is given with reference to the separate debt.”

§ 390. Upon the foreclosure of a mortgage, by a bill in equity, the defendant may set off a demand he has against the complainant which would be a proper subject of set-off in a suit brought by the complainant at law, to recover the amount due upon his mortgage. (a)

In the matter of the Receivers of the Globe Ins. Co., (2) the petitioners obtained a loan of money from the insurance company in order to erect a building upon their lot of land; and to secure the re-payment of the same, they gave to the company their bond and mortgage of the premises. As soon as the building was erected it was insured in the office of the company. It was afterwards destroyed by fire, and the company at the same time rendered insolvent. The petitioners now prayed that the amount of the loss upon the policy of insurance might be set off against the bond and mortgage. The vice chancellor (M’Coun) said: “As between the company and the assured, there would be a clear right of set-off at law. In a suit upon the bond by the Globe Insurance Company, the petitioners might avail themselves of the present statutory provisions on the subject of set-off, and claim that the loss which had accrued upon the policy should be deducted from the bond, and the balance only, considered the debt due from them. There are here all the requisites of a set-off: A demand arising upon contract, due to all the petitioners jointly in their own right—liquidated or capable of being ascertained by calculation—and existing and belonging to them at the time of commencing the suit, provided a

There must either have been a direct payment of a part of the debt, or an agreement that the sum proposed to be set off, should be received and credited as payment” (Dolman v. Cook, 1 McCarter’s N. J. R. 56; Bird v. Davis, Ib. 467).

§ 397 IN CASES OF INSOLVENCY. 

§ 397. The assignment of a judgment by an insolvent has been held to afford an equitable ground of set-off against it in the hands of the assignee, even in a case free from fraud.

In Merrill v. Souther, (a) Merrill filed a bill in chancery against Souther and Fowler, alleging that after a fieri facias on a judgment which he had obtained against Souther had been returned nulla bona, the latter had obtained a judgment against him for a smaller sum, and being insolvent, had fraudulently assigned it to his co-defendant Fowler, and praying for an injunction against the latter judgment, and for a final decree of set-off. The Court of Appeals of Kentucky, in reversing the decree of the Circuit Court which dismissed the bill with costs, said: “Although there is no proof of the alleged fraud, nevertheless, as there is, in our opinion, sufficient evidence of Souther’s insolvency at the date of the assignment, the decree seems to us to be erroneous. As Souther was insolvent when he obtained his judgment against Merrill, the latter had co instant, and of course at the time of the assignment an equitable right to pay the judgment, by setting off his own judgment against it.” *

In England, ever admitted a set-off founded upon the mere fact of insolvency. But it seems to be well settled, Judge Story’s doubt notwithstanding, that insolvency furnishes a ground for the interposition of equity, in cases over which otherwise there would be no jurisdiction; as in the case of a debtor who claims to set off a legal demand against his judgment creditor which he cannot enforce or have an adequate remedy for at law by reason of the insolvency. In Tuscumbia, Courtland and Decatur R. R. Co. v. Rhodes, 8 Ala. R. 206, Goldthwaite, J., in delivering the opinion of the Supreme Court of Alabama, said: “We think it clearly deducible from the general scope of these (English) decisions, that insolvency was recognized as a distinct equitable ground entitling the party to relief even in cases where both demands were purely legal. In the American courts, the cases are more numerous and quite as decisive, to show that the same principle obtains in them generally.”

For as money is sometimes worth more than its interest, and the payment of it when due is often of vital importance to the creditor, the rebate or discount of interest may be a poor compensation for the loss of prompt payment. On the other hand, if I owe an insolvent man 100 dollars, and I hold his bond for the same sum payable a week hence, neither equity nor good sense would demand that I should pay my money to him, with the certainty of losing that which is due from him to me. The insolvency constitutes a new ingredient in the case, and upon the principle of the bill quia timet, a court of equity will retain in my hands what I owe for my indemnity, unless my adversary will secure me by some other satisfactory indemnity. Nothing is more common, I think, than the application of this principle to cases in equity. $3899. The obligor in a bond, becoming surety for advances to the obligee, and being, after the insolvency of the obligee, compelled to pay the debt for which he

leading cases on the subject were adverted to, said: “What then was Rhodes’ equity against the railroad company when the assignment was made by reason of its insolvency? The difficulty in finding the appropriate answer to this question grows out of the apparent injustice on the one hand, of permitting the debtor corporation to receive the benefit of their debt when it is morally certain they never will discharge that for which Rhodes was sponsor, and which he has since paid. While, on the other hand, there seem to be no English precedents, independent of those referred to on the construction of the bankrupt acts, of retaining a debt presently due to answer one that will only become so at a future time. The cases decided upon the construction of the bankrupt statutes are nothing more than the recognition of a principle well known to the civil law, which permitted a creditor, having goods or effects in possession of one afterwards becoming insolvent, to retain them until the debt was paid. We do not intend, however, to draw upon the civil law for reasons to sustain a proposition, which, if it exists at all, is capable of elucidation from cases decided either at law or in equity, by those courts from which we are authorized to look for binding precedents. We think the cases cited and principles adverted to evince very satisfactorily that one who stands to another in the relation of a surety may, if his principal becomes insolvent, not only retain money in his hands as indemnity to secure himself against loss, but also, that personal chattels in the hands of the surety, upon bailment, may be retained for the same purpose. It seems clear that the entire equity of Rhodes rests upon the insolvency of the company, and that the existence of this fact introduced new relations between them, whereby the former was entitled to retain the debt due to the latter, independent of the manner in which it was created, until the company either relieved him from, or indemnified him against, his obligation. As this equity existed when the assignment was made, that of Sherrod is controlled by it; and the debt having subsequently been paid by Rhodes, he is entitled to the relief which he seeks.”

Ormond, J., in dissenting from the foregoing opinion, said: “Insolvency is doubtless a sufficient reason, in many cases, for the interposition of a court of chancery, and, as such, has been frequently recognized in this court—as where an insolvent man is seeking to coerce a debt from one to whom he is indebted, but which from some cause cannot be set off at law. As between the debtor and creditor, there can be no doubt of the power and the duty of chancery in such a case to interpose. But where third persons have acquired rights, different considerations arise, and, according to my notions of equity, it would be unjust in a court of chancery to interpose and deprive an assignee of his legal rights, unless there is a natural equity growing out of the transaction itself, of which it is just that the debtor should be permitted to avail himself. I can see none such in this case. The debts are not mutual in any sense of the term, nor can there be any pretence of an agreement for stoppage; nor is there any equity inherent in, or growing out of, the debt due from Rhodes to the railroad, which a court of equity can give effect to. It is the naked case of a set-off allowed against the assignee, which had no existence until long after the debt matured, which the debtor owed the company, and which had been before assigned.”

As the law favors suretyship, contracts affecting the surety are strictly construed (New Orleans Canal and Banking Co. v. Hagan, 1 La. Ann. R. 62).

Where goods were placed by a debtor in the hands of his surety, for the purpose of indemnifying him against certain debts, which he immediately paid off, it was held that the fact of the surety’s making the application of the fund to the payment of those debts, instead of handing it to the other for him to do it, as was stipulated in the contract, gave the principal debtor no right to convey his claim on the said surety in respect of these goods for the security of other debts, or make the surety again account for the value of them, without allowing him credit for the application of the fund made by him (Williams v. Howard, 5 Jones Eq. R. N. C. 38).

Where parties enter into a parol agreement, that in the event one becomes bound as surety for another, a debt owned by the latter shall go in satisfaction of the liability, the former acquires no equitable right to the indemnity until he actually becomes bound as surety, and an equity created by an appropriation or assignment of the debt by parol prior thereto to a third person, will prevail (Newby v. Hill, 2 Metc. ty. R. 580).

Where administrators of an insolvent estate, in an action by them against a person who was surety for the deceased, were entitled to judgment, it was held that, whether the debt for which the surety was liable was or was not due in the lifetime of the deceased, if it was then due, the defendant was entitled to be released from so much of the judgment as would satisfy the debt (Beaver v. Beaver, 28 Penn. St. R. 167, overruling Bosler’s Adm’rs v. Exchange Bank, 4 Barr. 82).

A surety who pays the debt and takes a conveyance of all the creditor’s interest in land mortgaged to secure it, becomes by substitution, in effect, the mortgagee for the security of his advances; and the debt and mortgage pass by a residuary clause in his will (U. S. Dig. vol. 25, p. 482). A surety cannot, either at law or in equity, call for an assignment of the claim against his principal, or be clothed by mere operation of law and upon principles of equity with the rights of an assignee, unless he has paid the entire debt of the creditor; a pro tanto assignment will not be allowed (Neptune Ins. Co. v. Dorsey, 3 Md. Ch. Decis, 834). Where a surety for several joint principals pays the debt and one of the principals dies, he may claim a dividend from the estate upon the entire debt, although he holds collateral security for his liability (West v. Bank of Rutland, 19 Vt. R. 403). Where a creditor sells personal property which the principal has mortgaged to him as collateral security, he is responsible to the surety for ordinary care and prudence in the sale and the application of the proceeds (City Bank v. Young, 43 N. H. 457).

R., as the equitable and beneficial owner of the bond, and the moneys secured thereby, and against the defendant as assignee, it might be declared that the plaintiff was entitled in equity to set off the moneys so advanced by the plaintiff to R. R., and the moneys paid by the plaintiff as the surety of R. R. in satisfaction of the promissory notes.

§ 401. But to entitle a party to such equitable relief in a case not provided for by the statute, he must under certain special provisions of the New York revised statutes. The 86th section of the statute, relative to the powers, duties, and obligations of trustees and assignees of the estates of non-resident, absconding, insolvent, or imprisoned debtors, authorizes a set-off of cross demands, where mutual credits had been given, as well as where mutual debts existed between the absent, insolvent, or absconding debtor and any other person, and where the debt or claim of such other person is of such a nature as to entitle him to a dividend of the estate of the insolvent or absentee. This provision is made applicable to the receivers of an insolvent corporation by the 42d section of the statute relative to proceedings against corporations in equity, and by the 72d section of the statute relative to the voluntary dissolution of incorporations. The 42d section gives to the receiver, appointed by the court upon an adversary proceeding against the corporation, all the powers and authority conferred, and subjects him to all the obligations and duties imposed upon receivers appointed in case of the voluntary dissolution of a corporation. And by the 72d section all the provisions of law in respect to trustees of insolvent debtors, the collection and preservation of the property of such debtors, etc., are declared to be applicable to receivers appointed upon such voluntary dissolution of a corporation. The 2d section of the act of Jan., 1836, for the more convenient adjustment of the affairs of certain insurance companies in the city of New York, rendered insolvent by the then late fire in that city, also provided that the receivers appointed under that act should be subject to all the obligations and duties imposed upon receivers under any law of the State. They were thus brought directly within this provision of the statute relative to the offset of claims arising from mutual credits, as well as mutual debts, between the trustees of an insolvent debtor and other persons. The right of set-off in this case, therefore, was the same that it would have been in the case of an assignment under the insolvent act, which is more extensive, even in suits at law, than it would be under the general provisions of the revised statutes relative to set-off in ordinary cases (Walworth, Chancellor, in Holbrook v. Receivers, etc., supra).

The language of the statute of New York, “in relation to set-off in the case of trustees of an insolvent debtor,” is the same as that of the English bankrupt act, which has been repeatedly held not only to embrace mutual debts, but also all credits and transactions ex contractu where the credit or contract must ultimately terminate in a debt, although the debt had not been liquidated or become due and payable at the time of the bankruptcy; and it extends the right of set-off to every such debt or claim, which the creditor of the bankrupt would have the right to prove and receive a general dividend for, under the commission. Hence, in Graham v. Russell, 5 Maule & Selw. 498, which was heard in the exchequer chamber, before the twelve judges, under this provision of the bankrupt act in relation to mutual credits, it was held that, in a suit brought by the assignees of the bankrupt upon an open policy against the underwriter, the latter might offset a debt due to him from the bankrupt, arising out of a different transaction. That case was very similar to the case of Holbrook v. Receivers of Am. Fire Ins. Co., supra.

(a) Wray’s Admr’s v. Furniss, 27 Ala. 471.

* In the above case, the bill was filed by the administrator and administratrix of Wray against Martin, administrator of Slatter, deceased, and Furniss. The bill alleged that Slatter sold and conveyed with warranty certain land to Wray, and that Wray executed promissory notes for the purchase money; that Wray took possession of the land, and held it until his death; that Slatter died insolvent; that Martin, the administrator of Slatter, having brought an action on two of the notes against Wray, the latter died during the pendency of the suit; that the suit having been afterwards revived against the administratrix of Wray, judgment therein was rendered against her; that a note for $2,000, given as aforesaid by Wray to Slatter in part payment for said land, had been transferred to Furniss, a citizen of New York; and that Furniss had brought an action on said note against the administratrix of Wray, and would recover a judgment at the next term of the court unless enjoined. The bill further alleged that, during the lifetime of Wray, the Montgomery Hall Company brought an action of ejectment against him to obtain possession of the land purchased by him from Slatter; that said suit was revived against his administrators after his death, and a judgment having been rendered therein in favor of the plaintiffs, they were put in possession of said land; that Slatter, in his lifetime, and his administrator, after his death, were informed of the pendency of said action of ejectment, and required to defend it; and that Slatter, at the time he sold and conveyed the land to Wray, had no legal title to it, but the title was in the said Montgomery Hall Company. The complainants therefore prayed that, as the covenants of title contained in Slatter’s deed had been broken, and his estate, by reason of its insolvency, unable to respond in damages, the judgment and suit at law might be perpetually enjoined. The defendant, in answer to the bill, alleged that the note for $2,000, held by him, “was executed for another and wholly distinct consideration growing out of another and wholly distinct transaction, which had no connection whatever with the purchase of the lots mentioned in the bill;” that said note was executed and delivered for certain other land purchased by Wray from Slatter. After the answer came in, the complainants filed an amended bill, in which, after admitting the purchase by Wray from Slatter, as stated in the answer, they alleged that all of the notes were executed on the same day, and were all given for the purchase money of all the land. Chilton, C. J., in delivering the opinion of the court, said: “That the notes were given on the same day does not of itself so connect them as to make them parts of the same transaction. The consideration was distinct, and does not become blended merely because the notes bear even date. The covenants in the deed from Slatter, alleged to have been broken, have no reference to, nor connection with, the note for which the note held by Furniss was given; nor with the note itself, so as to enable the court to work out an equity in favor of the complainants.”

§ 403 IN CASES OF INSOLVENCY.

§ 403. The plaintiff having purchased the defendant’s property, and promised in consideration thereof to pay a specific amount of the defendant’s outstanding debts, and to allow him a life annuity; a court of equity will, on proof of the defendant's insolvency, establish an equitable set-off in favor of the plaintiff against his liability for the annuity, on account of damages resulting from a breach of the defendant’s warranty of title to the property conveyed, money paid by the plaintiff at the defendant’s request outside of the contract,—board and other necessaries furnished, and professional services rendered as an attorney-at-law. But it is otherwise as to a demand for unliquidated damages arising out of a tort, and professional services rendered in suits by and against the plaintiff himself concerning the property. (a) *

Does an equity exist regarding them as distinct transactions? The estate of Wray has an equity against the estate of Slatter to the extent of the notes given for the lots to which there is a failure of title, and it has a demand against said estate for the residue; but, as to this residue, it is but a cross demand, existing in the form of damages, for a breach of the covenant contained in the deed. These damages are unliquidated, and could not ordinarily be the subject of set-off either in a court of law or equity. But it is insisted in the case before us, that an equity attaches to have the set-off allowed by reason of the insolvency of Slatter's estate. This would certainly be a good ground for equitable interposition as against Slatter’s estate. But, although the insolvency of one of the mutual debtors, existing at the time of filing the bill, would be a sufficient ground of equitable jurisdiction as between them, yet, where one of the mutual debts existing in the form of a note is assigned to a third person, it seems clear that the insolvency of the obligee, commencing after the obligor has notice of the assignment, can never attach as an equity against the note in the hands of the assignee, nor furnish in itself a ground for setting off against it the debt of the obligee to the obligor. For aught that appears, the assignment and notice of it accrued long before the insolvency; and as it is incumbent upon every complainant to show by his bill a title to the relief which he seeks, and none is shown here, the bill as to Furniss was properly dismissed.

§ 404. An equitable offset which the debtor to a bank had at the time the bank stopped payment is not altered by the appointment of a receiver. (a)

Mel and others v. Holbrook, was an application to the court to enjoin the defendant from prosecuting a suit at law against the complainants in the Superior Court of the City of New York. It appeared that one Graham, being the proprietor of a bank in the State of Florida, solicited the complainants for drafts on his mercantile house in New York, and, on receiving them, paying in the bank notes of the said bank. The drafts having been duly presented and accepted, afterwards and before they matured, and while the aforesaid mercantile house held most of the bank notes which had been received for the said drafts, together with other notes of the said bank received by said house in the regular course of defeat the pending suit upon so much of the annuity as had accrued, but balance his claims against his liability upon installments to become due in future. If the complainant had been evicted from the possession of the property sold to him under a paramount title, he might have recovered the counsel fees in the suit which resulted in his eviction, by way of damages for the breach of warranty of title. The counsel fees of the complainant, in suits to which he was a party, and which were brought by or against him in reference to the property after his purchase, could not be a charge against the defendant. But for the services rendered by the complainant, in suits for and against the defendant, he would be entitled to compensation from the defendant the same that he would from any other person for similar services. The fact that the complainant contracted to pay a specified amount of the defendant’s debts produced no legal obligation to attend to lawsuits or any other business for the defendant; and for all the services rendered by the complainant for the defendant, in and about his lawsuits, the defendant was legally liable to the complainant, and the complainant was entitled to have the same set off against his liability to the defendant.

§ 406. It is a general principle of equity that, when a party has a proper remedy at law, he cannot go into a 

(a) Holbrook v. Receivers of Am. Fire Ins. Co. 6 Paige R. 220.

* In the Matter of the Receivers of the Globe Ins. Co. 2 Edw. Ch. R. 625, the question arose whether the insolvency of the company and the placing of all its property and effects in the hands of receivers for the benefit of creditors, had taken away the right of set-off. It was held, that there was nothing in the various provisions of the statute of New York, in relation to the dissolution of insolvent corporations and the duties of receivers, which could have such an effect.

By the statute of New York, of Jan. 18th, 1836, it was declared that receivers should have all the powers and authority conferred, and be subject to all the obligations and duties imposed upon receivers under any law of the State, and by the general law in relation to receivers of insolvent corporations, they are placed upon the same footing as assignees or trustees of the estates of insolvent debtors. And in the enumeration of those powers and duties, and particularly in declaring that such trustees shall have power to sue in their own names, the right of set-off in the party sued is expressly provided for, taking care to restrict it to debts owing before public notice of the appointment of the trustees, or of the commencement of proceedings by which they become, by relation, vested with the estate; and where mutual credit has been given by any debtor, and any other person or mutual debts have subsisted between such debtor and any other person, the trustees are expressly authorized, without any suit or action being instituted, to set off such credits or debts, and to pay the proportion or receive the balance. A similar provision is contained in the English bankrupt law, in cases of mutual debts, or where mutual credits have been given, and it is the common practice to allow set-offs there—taking the balance as the debt really due, which the debtor of the bankrupt pays to the assignee, or, when the bankrupt is the debtor, upon which the creditor receives his dividend equally with other creditors. When rightly considered, there is nothing in all this that can militate against the principle of equality being equity among the creditors of a bankrupt or insolvent estate; for, where parties have had dealings so as to produce mutual debts or credits, or reciprocal demands growing out of the same transaction, it is the balance only which exists as the debt; and a set-off in such case is not a means of paying one debt in preference to other debts which the bankrupt or insolvent owes; for, to the extent of the demands set-off or compensated, there was no debt; from the moment they were contracted they extinguished each other. Hence, the operation of a set-off is not to pay, but to ascertain a debt made up of the difference between the amounts of respective debits and credits (M’Coun, V. C., in the Matter of the Receivers of the Globe Ins. Co. supra).

<br>

8. Where relief cannot be obtained at law.

§ 408. If a defendant in a court of law has a distinct and separate demand against the plaintiff, which is not a proper subject of set-off there, he cannot obtain relief in a court of equity unless the plaintiff is insolvent. His proper course is to pay the plaintiff’s demand, and then prosecute for his own. But it is otherwise if his claim arises out of the same transaction or contract as that of the plaintiff, so that in equity the plaintiff never had any right to recover against him. He is not obliged to pay an unjust demand, although he might recover a greater amount in damages in a suit instituted by himself. It must, however, be such a demand as he has a clear right to enforce against the plaintiff in the action.

9. Concurrent jurisdiction.

§ 409. “It is a clear principle of jurisprudence,

(a) Reed v. Bank of Newburg, 1 Paige R. 215.

§ 409 | CONCURRENT JURISDICTION. 461

that when there exist two tribunals possessing concurrent and complete jurisdiction of any question, that the jurisdiction of that tribunal is exclusive which has first possession of the subject matter of controversy.” (a) *

(a) King, Prest. in Slyhoof agst. Flitcraft, 1 Ashmead, 171.

* “When a court of law and a court of equity have concurrent jurisdiction of the matter in dispute, the court which takes jurisdiction, settles the matter conclusively” (Am. Ch. Dig. 8d ed. vol. 2, p. 551, citing Thompson v. Hill, 8 Yerg. 167; Flournoy’s Exrs. v. Halcomb, 2 Munf. 34).

In Simpson v. Hart, 1 Johns, Ch. R. 91, Chancellor Kent said: “It is a principle which prevails not only in our own, but in all other systems of jurisprudence, and has become a rule of universal law, and is founded in the soundest policy. It springs from that comity which is due from one court of concurrent jurisdiction in the given case to another; and from the necessity of putting an end to litigations which have been once heard and decided, and of preserving mutual harmony, respect, and confidence between the several tribunals concerned in the same administration of justice. I find no modern case in which chancery has taken cognizance, on the same grounds, of the very point which another court of competent authority in the case has considered and decided. Whenever the bill has been sustained, it has always been upon some new matter of equity not arising in the former case, or for some relief to which the powers of the court of law were not fully and effectually adequate.”

The court of chancery in England restrained the defendant from proceeding in a suit previously commenced in the court of sessions in Scotland (Bushby v. Munday, 5 Mad. R. 297). In that case, Sir John Leach admits that, by the act of union, the courts of Scotland are entirely distinct and independent jurisdictions, and says that the same principles would apply were the suits, which are sought to be enjoined, pending in any foreign jurisdiction. “Where a party is within the jurisdiction of this court, although the subject matter of the suit may be situated elsewhere, it may, by the ordinary process of injunction and attachment for contempt, compel him to desist from commencing a suit at law, either in this State or any foreign jurisdiction. But, although this court has the physical power to act coercively on the parties within its jurisdiction to that extent, it has frequently decided that it would not sustain an injunction bill to restrain a suit or proceeding previously commenced in a court of a sister State or in any of the federal courts. The same principle has been adopted by the Supreme Court of the United States (Diggs v. Wolcott, 4 Cranch, 179; McKim v. Voorhies, 7 Ib. 279). And I am not aware that any court of equity in the Union has deliberately decided that it will exercise the power, by process of injunction, of restraining proceedings which have been previously commenced in the courts of another State. Not only comity, but public policy, forbids the exercise of such a power. If this court should sustain an injunction bill to restrain proceedings, previously commenced in a sister State, the court of that State might retaliate upon the complainant who was defendant in the suit there; and, by process of attachment, might compel him to relinquish the suit subsequently commenced here. By this course of proceeding, the courts of different States would indirectly be brought into collision with each other in regard to jurisdiction; and the rights of suitors might be lost sight of in a senseless struggle for what might be considered the legitimate powers and rights of courts” (Walworth, Chancellor, in Mead v. Merritt, 2 Paige, 402).

<br>

§ 410. Therefore, where courts of law and equity have concurrent jurisdiction over a question, and it receives a decision at law, equity can, in general, no more re-examine it than courts of law in a similar case could re-examine a decree of a court of equity.

In an early case in New York, (a) Chancellor Kent maintained that the refusal of a court of law to allow a set-off, after a full consideration of all the circumstances of the case was res judicata, and conclusive and binding on all other courts of concurrent jurisdiction. But the New York Court of Errors afterwards, in the same case, (b) refused to concur in this view of the chancellor, but, on the contrary, held that decisions upon motion and summary application which did not admit of great discussion, or of being subject to a writ of error, were not final and conclusive, so as to amount to res judicata and a bar to a renewed consideration of the case in another court.

Accordingly, in Hackett v. Connett, (c) a bill

The case of Mead v. Merritt, supra, was as follows: A. who died in the State of Connecticut, was indebted to B., who assigned the claim to C. for a valuable consideration. An injunction which had been granted by a master in chancery, restraining the defendants from proceeding in Connecticut to recover the amount of this demand, was dissolved.

10. Burthen of proof on party making the set-off.

§ 411. A party seeking to make a set-off in equity beyond that given by the statute, must affirmatively show the existence of all those facts necessary to raise the equity. (a)

(a) Lockwood v. Beckwith, 6 Mich. R. 168.

* In Hackett v. Connett, supra, Vice Chancellor McCoun said: “The defendants insist upon the result of the motion in the Superior Court as conclusive upon the complainant. The grounds of denying the motion there do not distinctly appear. As far as the views of the court of law have been ascertained, the merits were not passed upon. The judges considered it a case more proper for a chancery suit. They declined interfering, although they had the matter fully before them upon affidavits, and were competent, in the exercise of their equity powers over judgments in their own court, to determine the question. Still whatever they may have intended, and whether they did or did not pass upon the merits of the application, it would not be a matter res judicata so as to preclude an inquiry in this court which has a concurrent jurisdiction.”

The concurrent jurisdiction of courts of equity embraces a large portion of the original jurisdiction inherent in the court, or first conferred upon it. It arises from one of two causes: Either the courts of law, although they have general jurisdiction in the matter, cannot give adequate, specific, and perfect relief, or, under the circumstances of the case, they cannot give any relief. The former occurs in all cases when a simple judgment for the plaintiff, or for the defendant, does not meet the full merits and exigencies of the case; but a variety of adjustments, limitations and cross claims are to be introduced and finally acted on; and a decree meeting all the circumstances of the particular case between the very parties is indispensable to complete distributive justice. The latter occurs, when the object sought is incapable of being accomplished by the courts of law; as, for instance, a perpetual injunction, or a preventive process to restrain trespasses, nuisances, or waste” (Story’s Eq. § 77).
