In Bullard v. Raynor (a) the plaintiff claimed as assignee of E. F. B. to recover of the defendant a balance of account between E. F. B. and the defendant. It appeared that in the fall of 1856, E. F. B. stated the account, presented it to the defendant, and demanded payment, which being refused, it was assigned by E. F. B., in March, 1857, to the plaintiff. In the account as stated by the plaintiff’s assignor, among other items therein allowed to the defendant as payment, was a note for $75.00 made by E. F. B.—payable to the order of one H—which was taken up by the defendant. The plaintiff contended that, as the note was usurious, the defendant could not avail himself of it as a payment. But it was held that the maker having stated the account including the note and thereby admitted the correctness of the charge, the plaintiff claiming as assignee of the maker could not set up the defense of usury. *

(a) 80 N. Y. R. 197.

* On the facts in this case, E. F. B. might by bill in equity have asserted the usury in this note, and defeated it as a set-off, notwithstanding the account between him and the defendant had become a stated account. But while it stood as a stated account as between him and the defendant, the assignee was concluded by it, and could not assail it successfully so as to let in the defense of usury (Ib. per Mullen, J.)

“Usury is a defense personal to the party known as the borrower. He cannot transfer to another the right he has to allege and prove a demand to be usurious” (Ib.)

“No one but a party to a usurious loan or his heirs, devisees or personal representatives, can avoid a usurious contract on account of usury. Usury cannot be set up by a stranger to the original transaction. A purchaser from the borrower is not included in the term borrower, and cannot avoid a note or mortgage for usury” (Ib. Wright, J., citing Post v. the Bank of Utica, 7 Hill, 391; Rexford v. Widger, 2 Comst, 181; Schermerhorn v. Talman, 4 Kernan, 127).

“I think the assignee of the demand in suit can resist it for usury unless his assignor has by his acts in reference thereto precluded him. No rule is better settled than that the purchaser of property, charged with a usurious lien or claim, can allege the usury and defeat the claim when the purchaser sold discharged of such usurious lien” (Ib. Mullin, J., citing Post v. Dart, 8 Paige, 639; Shufelt v. Shufelt, 9 Ib. 137; Brooks v. Avery, 4 Comit, 225).

§ 605 DEMAND CANNOT BE SET OFF.

28. Demand once passed upon cannot be set off.

§ 603. If a party to a suit, either plaintiff or defendant, presents a demand which is legal and proper to be allowed, if supported by sufficient testimony, and the jury pass upon it and disallow it, such demand cannot be received, or set off in another suit between the same parties. (a)

§ 604. The rule has been stated thus: “If the same question is submitted to a jury in a first action, and the evidence in the last, if it had been given in the first, would have been equally available as in the last, to entitle the party to recover under the state of pleadings in both, then the verdict and judgment are an absolute bar. But where, from the number of the plaintiffs or defendants in the first suit, the testimony relied on in the second is sufficient to authorize a recovery in such second action, but could not have produced a different result in the first, the failure of the plaintiffs in the one suit is no bar to their recovery in the other, although it is for the same cause of action for which they attempted to recover in the first suit.” (4)

§ 605. The early English cases held that if, at the trial, the defendant attempted to prove his cross demand, and did not succeed, he could not afterwards maintain an action for the amount; and could not, of course, maintain an action for what he had succeeded in proving as a set-off in a former suit against him. If, however, the set-off proved in the former suit was more

* Where a matter is improper by way of set-off, and a party introduces it, and goes into an investigation with the view to make it available, and it is submitted and passed upon by the jury, it cannot be again brought up in a suit by such defendant, and if it is, the former suit and trial may be pleaded in bar of a recovery (Wilder v. Case, 16 Wend. 583). It has been held as a general proposition, that where a claim, whether it can legally be set off or not, is pleaded and not objected to, and the jury pass upon it, the consent of the parties thus to be implied, will take away the error, and it then becomes a bar to a subsequent suit (King v. Fuller, 8 Caines, 152).

“In the plea that the plaintiff had once set off his demand in a former suit, it is not necessary to distinguish by the plea, nor is it important in evidence whether the first action was upon contract or tort; nor is it material what was the nature of the matter introduced as a set-off, whether

<br>

### --- Page 0715 ---

§ 606 DEMAND CANNOT BE SET OFF. 657

McLean v. Hugarin (a) was an action of trover to recover the value of a spinning-wheel. The defendant pleaded a former action for the same cause, in which the present plaintiff, being defendant, set off the present demand, which was tried in that action. The court said: “Although the demand in this case sounds in tort, and might not, in strictness, have been admissible as a set-off on the former trial, yet, if it were admitted without objection, and has been once tried, that judgment is conclusive.”

In Sherman v. Crosby (4), what was apparently the separate debt of one defendant was offered to be set off against the joint debt of both. The plaintiff objected, upon the ground of the insufficiency of the proof only; and on its being ruled against him, submitted to a non-suit. On a motion to set aside the nonsuit, the court said it was too late to object that it was a separate debt of one defendant; because, if the objection had been made at the time, the defendants might have shown that the payment by Crosby was in fact made by him and his co-defendant as partners, and out of the partnership funds.

In M’Kinney’s Adm’r v. Robinson, (c) a motion was made to set aside a judgment, on the ground that the matter offered by way of set-off by the defendant be this was matter of contract or of wrong. It is enough that it has once been set off and tried, submitted or stated for trial, and passed into the hands of a court or jury in the form of a set-off, for the purpose of being determined; or that any part of the entire demand claimed has thus been dealt with before. And where a judgment is insisted on as a set-off, and submitted to, and passed upon by a jury, whether the same be allowed or not, the judgment is extinguished and the plaintiff concluded; and if the plaintiff subsequently sue out an execution upon such judgment, he is a trespasser” (Cowen’s Tr. 3d ed. vol. 2, pp. 169, 170).

§ 607. In order to take the case out of the operation of the rule, the fact must appear affirmatively that the jury could not legally have allowed the defense. (a)

In Bull v. Hopkins, (6) Hopkins sued Bull, and declared for money paid and laid out for the use of the defendant. The defendant pleaded non-assumpsit, and that the same demand had been pleaded by way of set-off to a suit brought by Bull against Hopkins. It appeared that the set-off had been exhibited at the former trial, and was proved and rejected by the jury, because it was for a demand not then due. The court held that as it was for a demand which accrued subsequent to the former trial, it could not have been legally set off, and that, therefore, that trial was not a bar.

§ 608. Where, in an action upon several distinct indebtednesses, a set-off is allowed, the law presumes the amount to have been allowed ratably upon each of the indebtednesses. (c)

§ 616 DOES NOT WAIVE PREVIOUS DENIAL. 661

32. Withdrawal of set-off.

§ 614. A set-off being in the nature of a cross-action, may be withdrawn in analogy to suffering a non-suit when the evidence is found to be too weak to support it. But like a non-suit, the withdrawal of it ought to be explicit. (a) *

§ 615. The court may, in its discretion, allow items of set-off that have been withdrawn to be again filed.

33. Plaintiff by pleading payment, does not waive previous denial.

§ 616. A plaintiff by pleading payment of a set-off does not waive the benefit of a previous denial, but it is incumbent upon the defendant to prove his set-off. (c)

The attitude of resistance. He opposes the action of his adversary and endeavors to defeat the suit. If the plaintiff voluntarily comes and withdraws his suit, it is all the defendant can ask. Everything is accomplished that would be attained by his successful defense. But this law makes him an actor as well as the plaintiff. If his matter of set-off be larger than the plaintiff's demand, he stands in the attitude of plaintiff, and has all the rights of a plaintiff. So soon as the plea of set-off is made, exhibiting such excess of demand, it becomes a cross-action, and the party pleading is in fact plaintiff and the other is defendant, however they may be named in the proceeding. The defendant, in an ordinary case, can with as much reason dismiss the plaintiff's suit against him, as a plaintiff before a justice of the peace can do so in a case where the defendant has pleaded a set-off larger than his demand. The party to whom the balance is due has as much right to the decision of the issue in his favor, in the latter, as in the former case. It is not so, at common law, where the plea of set-off is filed; because, although a cross-action, it is purely defensive. All it aims at is to defeat the suit.

### --- Page 0720 ---

662 PLEADING. § 617

34, Defendant not precluded from relying upon other defense.

§ 617. Although a party files a set-off it does not preclude him from relying upon any other just defense on the trial of the cause. A special plea of set-off without any traverse of the plaintiff's demand, or any other plea denying it, might be considered as admitting it. This would, perhaps, be its legal effect. But a notice of set-off in general contains, either actually or by intendment of law, a denial of the plaintiff’s demand.

(a) Price v. Combs, 7 Halst. 188.  
(b) Morgan v. Boone, 1 J. J. Marsh. 585.
